title: Visualisation and Exploratory Analysis
text:
Choropleth Classification Schemes
A choropleth needs to bin a continuous variable into a small number of colour classes. geolattice.spatial_statistics.viz.choropleth offers three schemes (delegating to mapclassify when installed): quantiles (equal count per class), equal interval (equal value width per class), and natural breaks / Fisher-Jenks (classes chosen to minimise within-class variance).


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5.2))
for ax, scheme in zip(axes, ["quantiles", "equal_interval", "natural_breaks"]):
    choropleth(counties, "Dia_pct", scheme=scheme, k=5, ax=ax, cmap="YlOrRd")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()











Code
import mapclassify
for scheme, cls in [("Quantiles", mapclassify.Quantiles(counties["Dia_pct"], k=5)),
                     ("Equal interval", mapclassify.EqualInterval(counties["Dia_pct"], k=5)),
                     ("Natural breaks", mapclassify.FisherJenks(counties["Dia_pct"], k=5))]:
    counts = pd.Series(cls.yb).value_counts().sort_index()
    print(f"{scheme:16s} bin edges: {np.round(cls.bins, 2)}  |  counties per class: {counts.tolist()}")


Quantiles        bin edges: [ 7.24  7.87  8.48  9.32 12.44]  |  counties per class: [44, 43, 43, 44, 43]
Equal interval   bin edges: [ 7.18  8.49  9.81 11.12 12.44]  |  counties per class: [40, 90, 65, 19, 3]
Natural breaks   bin edges: [ 7.14  8.14  9.08 10.16 12.44]  |  counties per class: [38, 71, 60, 34, 14]


Quantiles always give five visually similar-sized colour patches (43-44 counties each) regardless of how the underlying values are distributed: good for showing rank, poor for showing magnitude gaps. Equal-interval classes are easy to interpret (“each class spans about 1.3 percentage points”) but can leave some classes nearly empty if the data are skewed. Natural breaks looks for real gaps in the data and tends to isolate genuine outliers into their own class. None of the three is “correct”: they answer different questions, and switching schemes is often enough to change which counties look like the extreme ones on the map.

title: Visualisation and Exploratory Analysis
text:
The Moran Scatterplot
Moran’s I (formally defined in Chapter 2.4) has a geometric interpretation: it is the slope of the best-fit line through a scatterplot of each region’s value against the (row-standardised) average of its neighbours, the spatial lag. moran_scatter builds this plot directly from a MoranResult (or from raw y, w).


Code
res = Moran(counties["Dia_pct"], w, permutations=999, seed=1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 6))
moran_scatter(res, ax=ax, color=C["blue"], alpha=0.7, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"Moran's I (the fitted slope) = {res.I:.4f}")









Moran's I (the fitted slope) = 0.2398



A labelling caveat: centred, not standardised
The scatterplot’s axis labels (“z (standardized attribute)”) describe the x-axis as standardised, but the implementation only centres the variable (subtracts the mean): it does not divide by the standard deviation. This is a real, checkable discrepancy between the label and the code:


Code
import inspect
from geolattice.spatial_statistics.viz.moran import moran_scatter as _ms
src_line = [l for l in inspect.getsource(_ms).splitlines() if "z = y - y.mean()" in l][0]
print("moran_scatter source line:", src_line.strip())
print(f"std(z) as actually plotted: {(counties['Dia_pct'] - counties['Dia_pct'].mean()).std():.4f}  (not 1.0)")


moran_scatter source line: z = y - y.mean()
std(z) as actually plotted: 1.2018  (not 1.0)


The consequence is cosmetic, not statistical: Moran’s I itself (the slope) is invariant to this scaling choice, so the number reported is unaffected. What changes is the axis units: the horizontal spread in the figure above is in percentage points of diabetes prevalence, not in standard-deviation units as the label implies. When reporting this plot, relabel the axis as “centred attribute” or divide by z.std() before plotting if a true z-score axis is wanted.


The island on the axis
Nantucket County (Chapter 2.2, Section 9) has zero Queen neighbours, so its row-standardised spatial lag is exactly \(0\) by construction: every island sits exactly on the horizontal axis of this plot, regardless of its own value.


Code
z_all = counties["Dia_pct"].to_numpy() - counties["Dia_pct"].mean()
lag_all = w.lag(z_all)
island_idx = w.islands()[0]
print(f"Nantucket: z = {z_all[island_idx]:.3f}, lag = {lag_all[island_idx]:.6f}")

on_axis = np.isclose(lag_all, 0.0)
print(f"counties with lag exactly 0 (islands only): {on_axis.sum()} -> {counties.loc[on_axis, 'COUNTY'].tolist()}")


Nantucket: z = -1.299, lag = 0.000000
counties with lag exactly 0 (islands only): 1 -> ['Nantucket County']


A county with lag exactly \(0\) contributes nothing to the slope in either the “high” or “low” neighbourhood direction: it is neither confirmed nor contradicted by its (non-existent) neighbours. Section 5’s quadrant count below correctly excludes it from all four quadrants rather than assigning it arbitrarily.

title: Visualisation and Exploratory Analysis
section: Reading the Quadrants for a Health Outcome
text:
Reading the Quadrants for a Health Outcome
The Moran scatterplot splits into four quadrants around the origin, and for a health-outcome variable like Dia_pct each has a distinct, actionable reading:








Quadrant
Condition
Reading for Dia_pct




HH (high-high)
above-average county, above-average neighbours
A high-prevalence region: supports a regional public-health intervention, not a single-county one


LL (low-low)
below-average county, below-average neighbours
A low-prevalence region: a candidate for understanding protective regional factors


HL (high-low)
above-average county surrounded by below-average neighbours
A local outlier: investigate a county-specific cause (access to care, local demographics) or a data-quality issue


LH (low-high)
below-average county surrounded by above-average neighbours
A possibly protective pocket within a high-prevalence region: worth understanding what is different locally





Code
quad_names = np.full(len(z_all), "on-axis (island)", dtype=object)
quad_names[(z_all > 0) & (lag_all > 0)] = "HH"
quad_names[(z_all < 0) & (lag_all < 0)] = "LL"
quad_names[(z_all > 0) & (lag_all < 0)] = "HL"
quad_names[(z_all < 0) & (lag_all > 0)] = "LH"
counts = pd.Series(quad_names).value_counts()
counts


LL                  72
HH                  62
HL                  41
LH                  41
on-axis (island)     1
Name: count, dtype: int64


The clear majority of counties fall in the self-reinforcing HH/LL quadrants (62 + 72 = 134 of 217, 62%), which is exactly what a positive, significant Moran’s I predicts: but the plot also flags 41 HL and 41 LH counties whose local story runs against their region. Chapter 2.5 gives each of those counties a formal significance test (most will turn out to be indistinguishable from noise); for now, the scatterplot is a map of candidates for closer inspection, not a list of confirmed local outliers.

But the single most extreme county, Bronx County, NY (\(Dia\_pct = 12.44\), the highest in the dataset), is actually an HL outlier: its own value is far above average, yet its Queen neighbours average below the region mean. title: Visualisation and Exploratory Analysis
text:
Summary and Conclusions
This chapter turned Chapter 2.1’s raw map into two structured exploratory tools.

What we did

Compared quantile, equal-interval, and natural-breaks choropleth classification, and confirmed they can tell visually different stories from the same data.
Built the Moran scatterplot and confirmed its slope equals the Moran’s I computed formally in Chapter 2.4 (0.240).
Found and documented a real labelling discrepancy: the plot’s x-axis says “standardized” but the implementation only centres the data: the slope (and hence Moran’s I) is unaffected, but the axis units are not what the label claims.
Showed that the one island in the data (Nantucket) sits exactly on the horizontal axis by construction, and should be excluded from quadrant counts rather than assigned one.
Read the four quadrants (HH/LL/HL/LH) as actionable categories for a health outcome, and counted 62 HH, 72 LL, 41 HL, 41 LH counties.
Checked that the most extreme-valued counties are also the ones driving the positive slope (all in HH/LL), rather than being isolated high-leverage outliers.



Practical takeaways

Choropleth classification is not neutral: pick (and report) the scheme deliberately, and consider showing more than one when values are skewed.
The Moran scatterplot’s slope is Moran’s I; treat the two as the same fact in two different forms, not as independent evidence.
Always check a plotting function’s axis labels against its actual computation before reporting a figure, this library’s own moran_scatter is a concrete example of where the two can silently diverge.



Next steps
Chapter 2.4 (Measuring Global Spatial Autocorrelation) gives the slope seen here a formal null distribution, a z-score, and a permutation p-value: and introduces Geary’s C, General G, join counts, and bivariate Moran’s I as complementary global measures.

title: Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Overview
Part 1 asked where events happen. Part 2 asks a related but distinct question about a different kind of data: given one value per areal unit, a county, a census tract, a zip code, are nearby units more alike than distant ones? This is spatial autocorrelation, and it is the single most consequential diagnostic in spatial data analysis: almost every method downstream of it (regression in Part 3, cluster detection in Part 4, disease mapping in Part 5) either assumes its absence or explicitly models its presence.
This chapter lays the conceptual groundwork before any statistic is computed:







Step
What we do




Concept
State Tobler’s first law and what “positive”, “negative”, and “no” autocorrelation mean


Distinction
Separate spatial dependence (values correlated with neighbours) from spatial heterogeneity (values vary by region for non-spatial reasons): and why conflating them breaks inference


MAUP
Introduce the modifiable areal unit problem: the boundaries we draw are not given by nature


Data
Load and inspect the five datasets used across Chapters 2.1-2.6


First map
Look at raw diabetes prevalence before measuring anything: the “eyeball test” that Chapter 2.3 formalises



By the end of this chapter you will have the vocabulary and the data in hand for Chapter 2.2, which builds the spatial weights matrices that every autocorrelation statistic in this Part depends on.

title: Spatial Autocorrelation
section: Tobler’s First Law and Spatial Dependence
text:
Tobler’s First Law and Spatial Dependence
Waldo Tobler’s (1970) informal but foundational statement:

“Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things.”

Formally, for an areal attribute \(Z_i\) observed at \(n\) regions, spatial autocorrelation measures whether the value at region \(i\) is statistically related to the values at nearby regions \(j\). Three qualitative patterns matter:

Positive autocorrelation: similar values cluster together (high near high, low near low): the typical pattern for most health, economic, and environmental variables, because whatever drives the outcome (climate, policy, shared infrastructure, social networks) itself varies smoothly over space.
Negative autocorrelation: dissimilar values are neighbours (a checkerboard): rarer, but arises from competitive processes (retail store locations, territorial ecology) or from mismatched administrative units overlaid on a smoother underlying process.
No autocorrelation: the value at one region carries no information about its neighbours: the complete spatial randomness of Part 1, transplanted to areal data.

Quantifying “positive”, “negative” and “none” is the job of Moran’s I and its relatives (Chapter 2.4); this chapter only fixes the vocabulary.

Why this matters for inference
Ordinary statistical inference, confidence intervals, p-values, standard errors, assumes observations are independent. Spatial autocorrelation violates that assumption directly: neighbouring counties are not independent draws, so the effective sample size is smaller than \(n\). Ignoring this:

Inflates apparent significance. Standard errors computed under independence are too small, so p-values are too small and confidence intervals too narrow.
Biases coefficients in a regression if the autocorrelation reflects an omitted spatially-structured driver correlated with the included covariates: not just a nuisance, but a source of bias (Part 3’s central topic).

Testing for autocorrelation is therefore not an optional extra step; the rest of this Part treats it as the first thing to check about any areal dataset.

title: Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Spatial Dependence vs. Spatial Heterogeneity
Two distinct phenomena can produce the same looking map, clusters of high values next to each other, for completely different reasons, and the distinction matters for what to do about it.









Spatial dependence
Spatial heterogeneity




Mechanism
The value at \(i\) genuinely depends on (or shares a process with) its neighbours
The process generating \(Z_i\) varies systematically by location, but each region is otherwise independent


Example
Disease spreads through contact between adjacent populations
A state-level policy variable that differs by state, with counties inheriting their state’s value


What autocorrelation statistics measure
Directly, this is what Moran’s I is built to detect
Indirectly, heterogeneity also produces positive autocorrelation, since the same policy value repeats within a state


Correct response
Model the spatial process (spatial lag/error models, Part 3)
Include the source of heterogeneity as a covariate or fixed effect



A significant Moran’s I does not by itself tell you which of these is at work: only that the map is not consistent with spatial independence. Chapter 2.5’s local statistics and Part 3’s regression diagnostics are the tools that start to separate the two explanations; for now, the practical lesson is to resist the jump from “I see clusters” to “there is spatial contagion” without further evidence.

title: Spatial Autocorrelation
section: Scale and the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem
text:
Scale and the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem
Every areal dataset in this Part reports a value per county, but counties are administrative artefacts, not natural units of the underlying process (disease risk, economic activity). The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP, met already in Part 1 Chapter 1.5) has two components that autocorrelation analysis inherits directly:

Scale effect: aggregating to larger units (counties → states) typically increases measured autocorrelation, because averaging over larger areas smooths out local noise and preserves broad-scale trend.
Zoning effect: for a fixed scale, redrawing the boundaries (alternative county-equivalent schemes) can change the measured autocorrelation even though nothing about the underlying process changed.

Both effects mean that “Moran’s I = 0.24” is a statement about this partition of this region: not a context-free property of diabetes prevalence. Chapter 2.6 returns to this with a concrete sensitivity check.

title: Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
First Look: Mapping Diabetes Prevalence
Before computing anything, plot the raw values. This is the “eyeball test”: does the map look like it has spatial structure at all? Chapter 2.3 does this properly with classification schemes and a Moran scatterplot; here it is enough to see that the answer is visually “yes”: there is a clear north-south gradient, with several adjacent high-prevalence counties in the lower-left (southwestern) part of the region.


Code

northeast.plot(column="Dia_pct", cmap="viridis", edgecolor="k", linewidth=0.2,
               legend=True, ax=axes[0], legend_kwds={"label": "Diagnosed diabetes (%)", "shrink": 0.7})
axes[0].set_title(f"Northeast: Dia_pct (n={len(northeast)})")
axes[0].set_axis_off()

atlantic.plot(column="Dia_pct", cmap="viridis", edgecolor="k", linewidth=0.15,
              legend=True, ax=axes[1], legend_kwds={"label": "Diagnosed diabetes (%)", "shrink": 0.7})
axes[1].set_title(f"Atlantic: Dia_pct (n={len(atlantic)})")
axes[1].set_axis_off()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









Both maps show the same qualitative pattern: prevalence is not scattered at random across counties, it forms recognisable regions of high and low values. Chapter 2.2 turns “which counties are near which” into a precise mathematical object (the spatial weights matrix W); Chapter 2.4 turns “looks clustered” into a number (Moran’s I) with a p-value.

title: Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Summary and Conclusions
This chapter set up the conceptual and data foundation for all of Part 2.

What we did

Stated Tobler’s first law and defined positive, negative, and no spatial autocorrelation.
Distinguished spatial dependence (a genuine neighbour effect) from spatial heterogeneity (region-level variation from a non-spatial source that still produces apparent clustering): a distinction that later chapters cannot resolve from Moran’s I alone.
Reviewed the modifiable areal unit problem’s scale and zoning effects, and why a reported autocorrelation value is tied to a specific partition of space.
Loaded and inspected the two primary datasets (diabetes_northeast, diabetes_atlantic), confirming a valid equal-area CRS and no missing data.
Mapped raw diabetes prevalence and observed visible, non-random spatial structure by eye.



Practical takeaways

Spatial autocorrelation is not a nuisance to test away; it is diagnostic information about how the data were generated, and it should be checked before any non-spatial statistical model is fit to areal data.
A clustered-looking map has at least two possible explanations (dependence vs. heterogeneity); a single global statistic cannot tell them apart.
Every autocorrelation number in this Part is conditional on the areal partition used to compute it (MAUP); treat it as a property of the data-and-boundaries pair, not of the underlying process alone.



Next steps
Chapter 2.2 (Spatial Weights) builds the W matrix that operationalises “near”: contiguity, distance-band, k-nearest-neighbour, kernel, and graph-based definitions: and examines what changes when the definition changes.

title: Hypothesis Testing and Model Extensions
text:
Overview
Chapter 1.3’s curves, Clark-Evans, G, F, J, K, L, and pair correlation, all pointed the same way: Buffalo crime is more clustered than CSR predicts. But none of those numbers came with a rigorous significance test, because the “expected under CSR” reference curves were theoretical formulas valid on an infinite plane, not calibrated to this window, this sample size, or the actual sampling variability of the estimator itself. This chapter closes that gap with Monte Carlo hypothesis testing, calibrates the test against patterns with known ground truth, and extends the analysis to two questions Chapter 1.3 deliberately set aside: does the clustering survive once the known intensity trend (Chapter 1.2) is accounted for, and do different crime types attract or avoid each other?







Step
What we do




Theory
Monte Carlo simulation envelopes; pointwise bands vs global tests; two more point processes


Calibration
Measure the test’s own size (false-positive rate) and power on patterns with known truth


CSR test
A formal, global Monte Carlo p-value for the real crime data


Inhomogeneous K
Ask whether clustering survives after removing the known citywide intensity trend


Cross-K
Ask whether Assault and Theft of Vehicle events co-locate more than chance predicts



By the end you will have a properly calibrated significance test for CSR, and the tools to distinguish genuine event-to-event interaction from an artefact of a non-constant intensity surface.

title: Hypothesis Testing and Model Extensions
text:
Monte Carlo Testing: Why Simulate?
The theoretical CSR curves used in Chapter 1.3 (\(\pi r^2\) for \(K\), \(1 - e^{-\lambda\pi r^2}\) for \(G\)/\(F\), and so on) describe the expected value of the statistic under CSR: but say nothing about how much that statistic varies from one CSR realisation to the next, in a finite window, with a finite sample size, under a particular edge correction. Two CSR patterns of the same size will not produce identical \(K(r)\) curves; the question is whether the observed pattern’s curve is further from the theoretical line than CSR’s own sampling variability would explain.
Conditional Monte Carlo testing answers this directly, using exactly the CSR-equals-binomial-process equivalence introduced in Chapter 1.1, Section 3.2:

Simulate \(m\) CSR patterns with the same event count \(n\), in the same window \(W\), as the real data.
Compute the summary statistic (e.g. \(L(r)\)) on each simulated pattern, giving \(m\) reference curves.
Compare the observed curve to the distribution of the \(m\) simulated ones.

This is the point-pattern analogue of the conditional permutation tests used throughout the package: compare envelope’s logic to the permutation machinery behind Part 2’s Moran’s I, or Part 4’s hot-spot statistics: the same idea (simulate the null, see where the data falls) applied to a different kind of statistic.

title: Hypothesis Testing and Model Extensions
text:
Simulating Alternatives to CSR
To calibrate a test, it helps to know the truth. Two processes with known, controllable structure:

Thomas cluster process
Introduced conceptually in Chapter 1.1; simulate_thomas(kappa, sigma, mu, window) implements it directly: unobserved “parent” events form a Poisson process of intensity \(\kappa\) (padded outside the window so that clusters near the edge are not truncated), and each parent produces \(\text{Poisson}(\mu)\) “offspring” scattered around it by an isotropic Gaussian of standard deviation \(\sigma\). The overall intensity is approximately \(\kappa\mu\); \(\sigma\) sets the spatial scale of each cluster.


Matérn hard-core (inhibition) process
simulate_matern_inhibition(intensity, radius, window) starts from a CSR pattern and deletes one member of every pair closer together than radius (formally: each event gets a random “priority” mark, and the lower-priority member of any too-close pair is removed): a simple model of events that compete for space and cannot occur too close together, the regular/inhibited counterpart to Thomas clustering.

title: Hypothesis Testing and Model Extensions
text:
Simulation Envelopes and Global Tests

Pointwise vs global envelopes
envelope(pp, statistic, nsim, alpha) returns, at every distance \(r\), the alpha/2 and 1 - alpha/2 quantiles of the statistic across the nsim simulated CSR patterns: a pointwise envelope, plotted as a shaded band. It is tempting to read “the observed curve leaves the band at \(r = 200\)” as “significant at \(r=200\)”, but this commits exactly the same error as reading a LISA map without a multiple-testing correction (Part 2): checking significance at 40 or 60 values of \(r\) simultaneously, each nominally at level \(\alpha\), inflates the overall false-positive rate far above \(\alpha\). A pointwise band is a useful visual, not a valid test on its own.


The MAD and DCLF test statistics
EnvelopeResult.test(kind) avoids the multiple-testing problem by collapsing the entire curve into a single number before comparing to the simulations, exactly once:

'mad' (maximum absolute deviation): \(T = \max_r \big|\,\hat{f}(r) - \bar{f}_{\text{sim}}(r)\,\big|\)
'dclf' (Diggle-Cressie-Loosmore-Ford): \(T = \int \big(\hat{f}(r) - \bar{f}_{\text{sim}}(r)\big)^2\, dr\)

Each simulated pattern gets its own \(T\) from the same formula (compared against the mean of the other simulations), giving a reference distribution of \(m\) values; the global p-value is the familiar \((1 + \#\{T_{\text{sim}} \geq T_{\text{obs}}\}) / (1 + m)\). This tests “is the whole curve, taken together, further from CSR than chance would produce?”: a single, valid hypothesis test.

title: Hypothesis Testing and Model Extensions
section: Beyond a Constant Baseline: the Inhomogeneous K Function
text:
Beyond a Constant Baseline: the Inhomogeneous K Function
Chapter 1.3’s \(K\), \(L\) and \(g\) all assumed a constant intensity \(\lambda\) when computing the CSR comparison. But Chapter 1.2 showed crime intensity is very far from constant across Buffalo. This matters: even a process with no genuine event-to-event interaction at all: an inhomogeneous Poisson process, with a smoothly varying \(\lambda(\mathbf{s})\) but independence between events: will make the homogeneous \(K(r)\) look inflated, simply because more points fall near each other wherever \(\lambda(\mathbf{s})\) happens to be high. Apparent “clustering” in Chapter 1.3 could, in principle, be nothing more than the known intensity trend of Chapter 1.2, with no additional interaction at all.
The inhomogeneous K function (Baddeley, Møller & Waagepetersen, 2000) tests this directly, by weighting each pair not by the constant \(\hat\lambda^2\) but by the product of the local intensities at that pair:
\[
\hat{K}_{\text{inhom}}(r) = \sum_{i \neq j,\; d_{ij} \leq r} \frac{1}{\hat\lambda(\mathbf{s}_i)\,\hat\lambda(\mathbf{s}_j)\,\gamma(\mathbf{v}_{ij})}.
\]
Under an inhomogeneous Poisson process, whatever the shape of \(\lambda(\mathbf{s})\), \(K_{\text{inhom}}(r) =
\pi r^2\), exactly as under ordinary CSR. So any remaining excess above \(\pi r^2\) after this adjustment is evidence of genuine interaction between events, not just a symptom of a non-constant background rate. k_inhom accepts a supplied intensity (an array, or any object with an .at() method such as a KDEResult from Chapter 1.2) or estimates one internally from the pattern itself with a leave-one-out kernel estimate.

title: Hypothesis Testing and Model Extensions
section: Interaction Between Types: the Cross-K Function
text:
Interaction Between Types: the Cross-K Function
For a marked pattern, cross_k(pp, mark_i, mark_j) asks a related but different question: do events of type \(j\) cluster around events of type \(i\), more than independence between the two types would predict?
\[
K_{ij}(r) = \frac{1}{\lambda_j}\, \mathbb{E}\big[\text{number of type-}j\text{ events within } r \text{ of a
typical type-}i\text{ event}\big].
\]
Under independent marking: each event’s type assigned independently of its location, so type \(j\) events are no more or less likely near a type \(i\) event than anywhere else: \(K_{ij}(r) = \pi r^2\), the same reference curve as before. \(K_{ij}(r) > \pi r^2\) suggests attraction between the types (they co-locate); \(K_{ij}(r) < \pi
r^2\) suggests avoidance.
A caveat that follows directly from Section 5: if both crime types share the same underlying citywide intensity trend (both are more common downtown, say), \(K_{ij}\) can appear elevated with no genuine type-to-type attraction at all: the homogeneous cross-K has exactly the same blind spot as the homogeneous K of Section 5. An inhomogeneous cross-K would be the rigorous next step; it is not implemented in this package, and Section 11 reports its homogeneous result with that limitation stated plainly rather than overclaiming a causal or type-specific interpretation.

title: Hypothesis Testing and Model Extensions
section: Calibrating the Test: Size and Power on Known Processes
text:
Calibrating the Test: Size and Power on Known Processes
Before trusting the test on real data, we check it on data whose truth is known: does it reject CSR about 5% of the time when the data really are CSR (the test’s size), and does it reject reliably when the data are genuinely clustered or genuinely regular (its power)? All three patterns here share the same \(n=80\) and unit-square window, so only the generating process differs.


Code
win_unit = Window.from_bounds(0, 0, 1, 1)
pp_csr_demo = simulate_csr(n=80, window=win_unit, seed=0)
pp_clus_demo = simulate_thomas(kappa=12, sigma=0.03, mu=7, window=win_unit, seed=0)
pp_reg_demo = simulate_matern_inhibition(intensity=300, radius=0.05, window=win_unit, seed=0)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4.6))
for ax, pat, title, col in zip(axes, [pp_reg_demo, pp_csr_demo, pp_clus_demo],
                               [f"Regular (Matérn), n={pp_reg_demo.n}",
                                f"CSR, n={pp_csr_demo.n}", f"Clustered (Thomas), n={pp_clus_demo.n}"],
                               [C["green"], C["grey"], C["red"]]):
    ax.scatter(pat.coords[:, 0], pat.coords[:, 1], s=18, color=col, edgecolors="k", linewidths=0.3)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_title(title)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()











Code
def rejection_rate(generator, n_reps=60, nsim=39, alpha=0.05, seed0=100):
    """Share of `n_reps` replicates for which the global MAD test rejects CSR at `alpha`."""
    rejections = 0
    for i in range(n_reps):
        pat = generator(seed0 + i)                          # seed for the replicate's own pattern
        env = envelope(pat, "L", nsim=nsim, seed=seed0 + i + 1000)   # independent seed for the null simulations
        rejections += env.test("mad") <= alpha
    return rejections / n_reps


size = rejection_rate(lambda s: simulate_csr(n=80, window=win_unit, seed=s))
power_clustered = rejection_rate(lambda s: simulate_thomas(12, 0.03, 7, win_unit, seed=s))
power_regular = rejection_rate(lambda s: simulate_matern_inhibition(300, 0.05, win_unit, seed=s))

calib = pd.DataFrame([
    {"scenario": "CSR (should be near the nominal 5%)", "reject at α=0.05": size},
    {"scenario": "Clustered (Thomas)", "reject at α=0.05": power_clustered},
    {"scenario": "Regular (Matérn)", "reject at α=0.05": power_regular},
]).set_index("scenario")
calib

The test’s size (its false-positive rate under the null it claims to control) sits close to the nominal 5%

with 60 replicates, sampling noise alone gives a margin of roughly \(\pm 3\) percentage points at this true rate, so this is consistent with correct calibration. Its power against both a genuinely clustered and a genuinely regular alternative is effectively 1.0: with this much departure from CSR, the global test never misses it. The same test, envelope(..., "L").test("mad"), is what Section 9 applies to the real data, now with a documented, checked false-positive rate behind it, not merely by analogy to the descriptive curves of Chapter 1.3.

title: Hypothesis Testing and Model Extensions
section: A Formal CSR Test on the Buffalo Crime Data
text:
A Formal CSR Test on the Buffalo Crime Data
We now apply exactly the same test to a 1,500-event subsample of the deduplicated Buffalo pattern (Chapter 1.3’s rationale for deduplication and subsampling both apply here: envelope’s cost scales with both the pattern size and the number of simulations).


Code
from pyproj import Transformer

tbl = pd.read_csv(DATA / "crime_data_2018.csv")
city = gpd.read_file(DATA / "buffalo_city.shp")
CRS_CORRECT = 26917
city_fixed = city.to_crs(4326).to_crs(CRS_CORRECT)
transformer = Transformer.from_crs(4326, CRS_CORRECT, always_xy=True)
x_m, y_m = transformer.transform(tbl["long"].to_numpy(), tbl["lat"].to_numpy())
coords_all = np.column_stack([x_m, y_m])
win_city = Window.from_gdf(city_fixed)
pp_dedup = PointPattern(coords_all, window=win_city, marks=tbl["incident_type"].to_numpy(),
                        clip=True).deduplicate()

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
pp_test = pp_dedup.subset(rng.choice(pp_dedup.n, 1500, replace=False))
r_range = np.linspace(0, 1500, 40)

env_real = envelope(pp_test, "L", nsim=99, r=r_range, seed=11)

print(f"working sample : n = {pp_test.n:,}")
print(f"global MAD test  : p = {env_real.test('mad'):.3f}")
print(f"global DCLF test : p = {env_real.test('dclf'):.3f}")
print(f"(smallest reportable p with 99 simulations: {1 / 100:.3f})")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.5))
env_real.plot(ax=ax, lw=2)   # EnvelopeResult.plot() colours the observed curve itself; no color= kwarg
ax.set_title("Buffalo crime vs. 99 simulated CSR patterns\n(L(r) − r; same n and window)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


working sample : n = 1,500
global MAD test  : p = 0.010
global DCLF test : p = 0.010
(smallest reportable p with 99 simulations: 0.010)









Both global tests reach the smallest p-value that 99 simulations can report: the observed curve never comes close to the simulated CSR envelope at any distance. Combined with the calibration in Section 8 (a test that correctly controls its false-positive rate and reliably detects real departures), this is now a properly supported conclusion, not just a descriptive impression: Buffalo crime departs from complete spatial randomness far beyond anything sampling variability could produce.

title: Hypothesis Testing and Model Extensions
section: Does Intensity Explain the Clustering? The Inhomogeneous K Function
text:
Does Intensity Explain the Clustering? The Inhomogeneous K Function
Section 9’s test, like all of Chapter 1.3, compared the data to a constant-intensity CSR baseline, which Chapter 1.2 already showed is the wrong baseline for this city. We now compare the homogeneous and inhomogeneous K functions on the same subsample, to see how much of the apparent clustering the known intensity trend can explain away.


Code
rng2 = np.random.default_rng(3)
pp_inhom = pp_dedup.subset(rng2.choice(pp_dedup.n, 2000, replace=False))

lam_at_events = intensity_at_points(pp_inhom, leave_one_out=True)   # kernel intensity, self excluded
k_hom = ripley_k(pp_inhom, r_range)
k_ih = k_inhom(pp_inhom, intensity=lam_at_events, r=r_range)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 5.5))
ax.plot(r_range, k_hom.estimate / np.where(k_hom.theoretical == 0, 1, k_hom.theoretical),
        color=C["red"], lw=2, label="homogeneous K / CSR  (Chapter 1.3's baseline)")
ax.plot(r_range, k_ih.estimate / np.where(k_ih.theoretical == 0, 1, k_ih.theoretical),
        color=C["blue"], lw=2, label="inhomogeneous K / CSR  (adjusts for the intensity trend)")
ax.axhline(1.0, color="k", ls="--", lw=1, label="CSR reference (either baseline)")
ax.set_xlabel("r (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("K(r) / πr²")
ax.set_title("Homogeneous vs. inhomogeneous K: how much does the\nintensity trend explain?")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

for i in [5, 15, 30, 39]:
    hr = k_hom.estimate[i] / k_hom.theoretical[i]
    ir = k_ih.estimate[i] / k_ih.theoretical[i]
    print(f"r = {r_range[i]:5.0f} m :  homogeneous {hr:.2f}×CSR   inhomogeneous {ir:.2f}×CSR   "
          f"(intensity trend explains {100 * (hr - ir) / (hr - 1):.0f}% of the excess)")









r =   192 m :  homogeneous 1.82×CSR   inhomogeneous 1.75×CSR   (intensity trend explains 10% of the excess)
r =   577 m :  homogeneous 1.51×CSR   inhomogeneous 1.32×CSR   (intensity trend explains 38% of the excess)
r =  1154 m :  homogeneous 1.36×CSR   inhomogeneous 1.13×CSR   (intensity trend explains 64% of the excess)
r =  1500 m :  homogeneous 1.31×CSR   inhomogeneous 1.09×CSR   (intensity trend explains 70% of the excess)


Adjusting for the known intensity surface reduces the apparent clustering at every distance, and the reduction is proportionally larger at long range than at short range: by \(r \approx 1{,}500\) m, the known citywide intensity trend explains most of the remaining homogeneous excess. But the inhomogeneous curve stays above 1 at every distance shown, especially at short range: so intensity variation is a real part of the story, but not the whole of it. Some genuine event-to-event clustering: beyond what “some places just have more opportunity” predicts: survives even after the adjustment, concentrated at the same short range that Chapter 1.3’s pair correlation function pointed to.

title: Hypothesis Testing and Model Extensions
section: Do Assault and Vehicle Theft Co-locate? The Cross-K Function
text:
Do Assault and Vehicle Theft Co-locate? The Cross-K Function
As a final, more exploratory question: does one crime type occur near another more than independence would predict? We compare Assault and Theft of Vehicle, two offence types with plausibly different typical settings.


Code
mask = np.isin(pp_inhom.marks, ["Assault", "Theft of Vehicle"])
pp_two = pp_inhom.subset(mask)
print(pd.Series(pp_two.marks).value_counts())

ck = cross_k(pp_two, "Assault", "Theft of Vehicle", r_range)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.5))
ax.plot(ck.r, ck.estimate / np.where(ck.theoretical == 0, 1, ck.theoretical), color=C["purple"], lw=2)
ax.axhline(1.0, color="k", ls="--", lw=1, label="independent marking")
ax.set_xlabel("r (m)"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$K_{ij}(r)\,/\,\pi r^2$")
ax.set_title("Cross-K: Assault events near Theft-of-Vehicle events\n(relative to independent marking)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

ratio_300 = float(ck.estimate[np.searchsorted(r_range, 300)] / ck.theoretical[np.searchsorted(r_range, 300)])
print(f"K_ij(r) at r = 300 m is {ratio_300:.2f}× the independent-marking reference")


Assault             398
Theft of Vehicle    173
Name: count, dtype: int64









K_ij(r) at r = 300 m is 1.92× the independent-marking reference


Assault and Theft of Vehicle events sit closer together than independent marking would predict, at every distance checked. This does not, on its own, establish that the two crime types attract each other: as Section 6 warned, and Section 10 just demonstrated directly for the single-type case, a shared underlying intensity trend (both offences more common in the same commercial and nightlife areas, say) can produce exactly this signature with no type-specific interaction at all. Confirming a genuine type-to-type effect would need an inhomogeneous cross-K, adjusting each type by its own estimated intensity: the natural next step, and, as noted, one this package does not yet implement.

title: Hypothesis Testing and Model Extensions
section: A Bridge to Time: Marks by Day of Week
text:
A Bridge to Time: Marks by Day of Week
Every function in this chapter has treated 2018 as a single, timeless snapshot. The data carry a day_of_week field that hints at a temporal dimension worth flagging, even though a full treatment is out of scope here (the companion hour_of_day field is a coarse 12-level bucket code, not a genuine 24-hour clock time, and is not reliable enough to analyse spatially).


Code
day_counts = tbl["day_of_week"].value_counts().reindex(
    ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"]
)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.bar(day_counts.index, day_counts.values, color=C["teal"])
ax.set_ylabel("incidents"); ax.set_title("Crime incidents by day of week, 2018")
plt.xticks(rotation=30, ha="right")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

weekend = tbl["day_of_week"].isin(["Saturday", "Sunday"])
print(f"weekday incidents : {(~weekend).sum():,}  ({100 * (~weekend).mean():.1f}%)")
print(f"weekend incidents : {weekend.sum():,}  ({100 * weekend.mean():.1f}%, vs 2/7 = 28.6% if days were equal)")









weekday incidents : 10,077  (72.0%)
weekend incidents : 3,924  (28.0%, vs 2/7 = 28.6% if days were equal)


Counts are fairly level across the week, with a modest lift on Friday and Saturday: plausible, and worth a formal test. Doing that test properly (e.g. a space-time K-function, or comparing the spatial pattern on weekdays against weekends) needs machinery this chapter does not have: a way to treat time as a genuine third dimension of the point process, not just another mark. That is exactly Part 9 (Spatio-Temporal Analysis), and this small chart is its first preview.

title: Hypothesis Testing and Model Extensions
text:
Summary and Conclusions

What we did

Explained why Monte Carlo simulation, not the theoretical CSR formulas alone, is needed to attach a valid p-value to a summary-function curve: and how conditional simulation licenses it.
Introduced two more point processes with controllable, known structure: Thomas clustering and Matérn inhibition.
Distinguished pointwise envelopes (a visual, vulnerable to the same multiple-testing problem as an unadjusted LISA map) from global MAD/DCLF tests (a single, valid p-value per pattern).
Calibrated the global test on synthetic data: its false-positive rate matched its nominal level, and its power against both clustered and regular alternatives was effectively 1.0.
Applied the calibrated test to the real Buffalo data: both global tests reached the smallest p-value 99 simulations can report.
Introduced the inhomogeneous K function, and showed that Chapter 1.2’s known intensity trend explains away much, but not all, of the apparent clustering, concentrated more at long range than short.
Introduced the cross-K function, found apparent co-location between Assault and Theft of Vehicle, and flagged, using the lesson just learned from the single-type case, that this cannot yet be told apart from a shared intensity trend with this package’s tools.
Previewed the temporal dimension (day of week) as a bridge to Part 9.



Practical takeaways

Never read significance off a pointwise envelope. Use EnvelopeResult.test('mad') or 'dclf' for a single, valid p-value; reserve the shaded band for visual intuition.
Calibrate before you trust. A test’s size and power on data with known truth is cheap to check and directly tells you whether to believe its output on data where the truth is exactly what you are trying to learn.
“Clustered” is not one claim: it is (at least) two. Elevated density where the process happens to have higher intensity is not the same phenomenon as events attracting each other conditional on that intensity. The inhomogeneous K function is how you tell them apart, and Section 10 shows both effects can be present at once, at different spatial scales.
The same logic applies to marks: an elevated cross-K between two event types is consistent with genuine interaction or with both types sharing a hot spot: distinguishing them needs an inhomogeneous cross-K, which is a documented gap here, not a result to be overclaimed.



Next steps
Chapter 1.5 (Integration with Areal Analysis, Pitfalls and Exercises) closes Part 1 by aggregating these same point events into the 35 Buffalo neighbourhood polygons, connecting point pattern analysis to the areal (lattice) methods of Part 2, working through the accumulated pitfalls of the whole Part, and a set of solved exercises.

title: First-order Analysis: Spatial Intensity
text:
Overview
Chapter 1.1 established that Buffalo’s 2018 crime events are not uniformly spread across the city: a first, informal impression from comparing the real data to a simulated CSR pattern. This chapter makes that impression precise: it estimates the intensity function \(\lambda(\mathbf{s})\), the local density of events per unit area, two different ways, and formally tests whether a constant intensity (CSR) is consistent with the data at all.







Step
What we do




Theory
Define intensity; contrast binned (quadrat) and smooth (kernel) estimators


Quadrat test
Partition the city into cells; test observed counts against the Poisson counts CSR predicts


Kernel density
Estimate a smooth intensity surface with edge correction for the irregular city boundary


Bandwidth
Compare a rule-of-thumb bandwidth (Scott) against one chosen by cross-validation


Relative risk
Map where one crime type is over- or under-represented relative to crime overall



By the end you will have quantified how far Buffalo crime departs from CSR in intensity alone (before any question of event-to-event interaction, which is Chapter 1.3’s job), and produced maps a crime analyst could actually use to prioritise areas.

title: First-order Analysis: Spatial Intensity
text:
What is Spatial Intensity?
Recall from Chapter 1.1 the intensity function
\[
\lambda(\mathbf{s}) = \lim_{|d\mathbf{s}| \to 0} \frac{\mathbb{E}\,N(d\mathbf{s})}{|d\mathbf{s}|},
\]
the expected number of events per unit area at location \(\mathbf{s}\). Under CSR, \(\lambda(\mathbf{s}) = \lambda\) is a single constant, estimated by the crude global rate \(\hat\lambda = n / |W|\) (Chapter 1.1’s pp.intensity). This chapter asks a sharper question: does \(\lambda\) vary over \(\mathbf{s}\), and if so, how?
Two estimation strategies, with different strengths:








Approach
Idea
Good for




Quadrat counts
Partition \(W\) into cells; compare observed counts to what a constant \(\lambda\) predicts
A formal test of CSR (a single p-value); simple, transparent


Kernel density
Smooth each event into a small “bump” of probability mass and sum the bumps
A continuous map of \(\hat\lambda(\mathbf{s})\); better for visual and comparative work



They answer the same underlying question at different resolutions: quadrat counts summarise intensity variation into one test statistic, kernel density spreads it into a full surface. Both are used below, and both point to the same conclusion.

title: First-order Analysis: Spatial Intensity
text:
Estimating Intensity: Two Approaches

The quadrat-count test of CSR
Divide the bounding box of \(W\) into an \(n_x \times n_y\) grid of cells. Under CSR, the count in cell \(c\) is
\[
O_c \sim \text{Poisson}\big(\lambda \cdot |c \cap W|\big),
\]
so the expected count is \(E_c = n \cdot |c \cap W| / |W|\): proportional to the area of the cell that actually lies inside the window, which matters for a city boundary as irregular as Buffalo’s. The Pearson chi-square statistic
\[
X^2 = \sum_{c} \frac{(O_c - E_c)^2}{E_c} \;\overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim}\; \chi^2_{k-1} \quad \text{under CSR}
\]
(with \(k\) the number of cells with \(E_c > 0\)) tests departure from a constant intensity. A companion statistic, the index of dispersion \(\text{IoD} = s^2_O / \bar{O}\) (variance over mean of the cell counts), is 1 under CSR, greater than 1 for clustered/overdispersed patterns, and less than 1 for regular ones: informal, but intuitive, and does not depend on the \(\chi^2\) approximation holding.
The chi-square approximation degrades when expected counts are small (a common rule of thumb: at least 80% of cells should have \(E_c \geq 5\)). quadrat_test also offers a Monte Carlo p-value (permutations=), drawing count vectors from the multinomial distribution implied by CSR: valid regardless of cell size.


Kernel density estimation
The kernel estimator replaces each event with a small bump of mass and sums them:
\[
\hat\lambda(\mathbf{s}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{h^2}\, k\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{s} - \mathbf{s}_i}{h}\right),
\]
where \(k\) is a kernel function (Gaussian, or the compact Epanechnikov kernel) and \(h\) the bandwidth. This package implements \(k\) as a product (separable) kernel, \(k(\mathbf{u}) = k_1(u_x)\,k_1(u_y)\), which makes the computation an efficient matrix product rather than an \(O(n \times n_{\text{grid}}^2)\) loop.


Bandwidth selection
\(h\) controls a bias-variance trade-off: small \(h\) tracks individual events closely (low bias, high variance, a speckled, noisy surface); large \(h\) averages over a wide area (low variance, high bias: a smooth surface that can wash out genuine local structure). Two choices are compared below:

Scott’s rule of thumb: \(h = \hat\sigma \cdot n^{-1/6}\), with \(\hat\sigma\) the mean coordinate standard deviation: fast, data-driven only through the pattern’s overall spread, and typically oversmooths clustered spatial data (it was derived for roughly Gaussian-shaped densities, not point-process clusters).
Likelihood cross-validation: choose \(h\) to maximise the leave-one-out log-likelihood \(\sum_i \log \hat\lambda_{-i}(\mathbf{s}_i)\): adapts to the data, but is well known to undersmooth clustered patterns (it keeps shrinking \(h\) to fit the tightest local clusters more closely).

Section 8 shows both are visibly biased in opposite directions here, which is itself the practical lesson: neither is a substitute for looking at the map.


Edge correction
Near the window boundary, a naive kernel estimate is biased low: part of the kernel’s mass would fall outside \(W\) (where there could not possibly have been an event), so the sum under-counts. kde(..., edge_correction=True) divides by the fraction of kernel mass that actually lands inside \(W\) (the “uniform” or Jones correction), which is exact for any window shape, not just rectangles: important for Buffalo’s non-convex boundary (Chapter 1.1, Section 10).

title: First-order Analysis: Spatial Intensity
text:
Rebuild the Point Pattern
Chapter 1.1 diagnosed a coordinate reference system error in the source shapefiles (declared UTM zone 11N; Buffalo is in zone 17N) and fixed it by reprojecting through longitude/latitude to EPSG:26917. We repeat that short, corrected build here so this notebook is self-contained; see Chapter 1.1 for the full diagnosis.


Code
from pyproj import Transformer

tbl = pd.read_csv(DATA / "crime_data_2018.csv")
city = gpd.read_file(DATA / "buffalo_city.shp")

CRS_CORRECT = 26917  # NAD83 / UTM zone 17N -- the correct zone for Buffalo (Chapter 1.1)
city_fixed = city.to_crs(4326).to_crs(CRS_CORRECT)
transformer = Transformer.from_crs(4326, CRS_CORRECT, always_xy=True)
x_m, y_m = transformer.transform(tbl["long"].to_numpy(), tbl["lat"].to_numpy())
coords_all = np.column_stack([x_m, y_m])

win_city = Window.from_gdf(city_fixed)
pp_all = PointPattern(coords_all, window=win_city, marks=tbl["incident_type"].to_numpy(), clip=True)

print(pp_all)
print(f"global (crude) intensity : {pp_all.intensity * 1e6:.2f} events / km²")

text:
Quadrat Analysis of Crime Intensity
We start with an \(8 \times 8\) grid over the city and a Monte Carlo p-value (199 multinomial simulations) alongside the analytical \(\chi^2\) approximation.


Code
qd = quadrat_test(pp_all, nx=8, ny=8, permutations=199, seed=1)

print(qd.summary())
p_analytic = "< 0.0001" if qd["p_value"] < 1e-4 else f"= {qd['p_value']:.4f}"
display(Markdown(
    f"**Index of dispersion = {qd['index_of_dispersion']:.1f}**: the variance of cell counts is "
    f"{qd['index_of_dispersion']:.0f} times the mean. Under CSR this ratio would be 1. Both the analytical "
    f"$\\chi^2$ test (p {p_analytic}) and the Monte Carlo test (p = {qd['p_mc']:.3f}, the smallest value 199 "
    "permutations can report) reject CSR decisively."
))


Quadrat test of CSR
===================

  df                   57

Index of dispersion = 166.9: the variance of cell counts is 167 times the mean. Under CSR this ratio would be 1. Both the analytical \(\chi^2\) test (p < 0.0001) and the Monte Carlo test (p = 0.005, the smallest value 199 permutations can report) reject CSR decisively.

section: Kernel Density Estimation of Crime Intensity
text:
Kernel Density Estimation of Crime Intensity
kde returns a KDEResult holding the surface on a regular grid, scaled so it integrates to (approximately) the event count \(n\): a useful sanity check on any kernel implementation.

h_scott = bandwidth_scott(pp_all)

      f"{100 * (kd.integral / pp_all.n - 1):+.1f}%: discretisation/edge-correction error)")

title: First-order Analysis: Spatial Intensity
text:
Bandwidth Selection in Practice
bandwidth_cv maximises leave-one-out likelihood over a geometric grid of candidate bandwidths (subsampling large patterns for speed: the default cap is 5,000 events, comfortably above what is needed to locate the optimum). We compare it against Scott’s rule.


Code
h_cv, candidates, scores = bandwidth_cv(pp_all, seed=1)

print(f"Scott's rule            : h = {h_scott:.0f} m")
print(f"Likelihood CV           : h = {h_cv:.0f} m")
print(f"ratio (Scott / CV)      : {h_scott / h_cv:.2f}×")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.2))
ax.plot(candidates, scores, "o-", color=C["blue"], ms=4)
ax.axvline(h_cv, color=C["red"], ls="--", label=f"CV optimum: {h_cv:.0f} m")
ax.axvline(h_scott, color=C["grey"], ls=":", label=f"Scott's rule: {h_scott:.0f} m")
ax.set_xlabel("bandwidth h (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("leave-one-out log-likelihood")
ax.set_title("Cross-validation score by bandwidth")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


Scott's rule            : h = 580 m
Likelihood CV           : h = 136 m
ratio (Scott / CV)      : 4.27×











Code
h_mid = float(np.sqrt(h_cv * h_scott))   # a visual midpoint on a log scale, for contrast only
bandwidths = {"Cross-validation (undersmooths)": h_cv, "Geometric midpoint": h_mid,
              "Scott's rule (oversmooths)": h_scott}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 5.6))
for ax, (label, h) in zip(axes, bandwidths.items()):
    k = kde(pp_all, bandwidth=h, grid_size=180)
    im = ax.imshow(k.density * 1e6, origin="lower", extent=k.extent, cmap="inferno")
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.04, label="events / km²")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_title(f"{label}\nh = {h:.0f} m")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()









The contrast is exactly what the theory in Section 3.3 predicts: the cross-validation bandwidth resolves many small, distinct hot spots: plausibly true local structure, but also plausibly some noise, since likelihood CV is known to undersmooth clustered spatial patterns; Scott’s rule washes almost everything into two or three broad regions, useful for a citywide overview but too coarse to act on locally. Neither is automatically “right”: the geometric midpoint is shown only as a visual compromise, not a principled recommendation. In practice, report the bandwidth used, and show at least two to let the reader judge: exactly as this section does.

title: First-order Analysis: Spatial Intensity
text:
Relative Risk: Comparing Crime Types
A map of where crime happens is dominated by where people and property are. A sharper operational question is: where is one crime type over-represented relative to crime overall? relative_risk(cases, controls) answers this with the ratio of two kernel density estimates: cases (e.g. Assault) against controls (every other incident type): so that areas with generally high crime no longer automatically dominate the map.


Code
assault = pp_all.by_mark("Assault")
other = pp_all.subset(pp_all.marks != "Assault")
print(f"Assault (cases)      : n = {assault.n:,}")
print(f"other crime (control): n = {other.n:,}")

rr = relative_risk(assault, other, bandwidth="scott", grid_size=180, log=True)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 7))
vmax = np.nanmax(np.abs(rr.density))
im = ax.imshow(rr.density, origin="lower", extent=rr.extent, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-vmax, vmax=vmax)
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.04, label="log relative risk (Assault vs. rest)")
city_fixed.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="k", lw=0.4)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_title("Where is Assault over- or under-represented\nrelative to crime overall?")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"log relative risk range: [{np.nanmin(rr.density):.2f}, {np.nanmax(rr.density):.2f}]")
print("positive (red) = Assault more common here than the citywide mix would predict;"
      " negative (blue) = less common")


Assault (cases)      : n = 2,765
other crime (control): n = 11,183









log relative risk range: [-1.42, 0.81]
positive (red) = Assault more common here than the citywide mix would predict; negative (blue) = less common


Repeating this for a second type shows the surfaces genuinely differ by crime type, not just by population density (which would make every relative-risk map look the same).


Code
tov = pp_all.by_mark("Theft of Vehicle")
other_tov = pp_all.subset(pp_all.marks != "Theft of Vehicle")
rr_tov = relative_risk(tov, other_tov, bandwidth="scott", grid_size=180, log=True)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6.4))
for ax, r, title in zip(axes, [rr, rr_tov], ["Assault vs. rest", "Theft of Vehicle vs. rest"]):
    vmax = np.nanmax(np.abs(r.density))
    im = ax.imshow(r.density, origin="lower", extent=r.extent, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-vmax, vmax=vmax)
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.04, label="log relative risk")
    city_fixed.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="k", lw=0.4)
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_title(title)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

corr = np.corrcoef(np.nan_to_num(rr.density.ravel()), np.nan_to_num(rr_tov.density.ravel()))[0, 1]
print(f"correlation between the two log-relative-risk surfaces: {corr:.3f}  "
      "(well short of 1: these are genuinely different spatial patterns, not both just 'more crime')")









correlation between the two log-relative-risk surfaces: 0.298  (well short of 1: these are genuinely different spatial patterns, not both just 'more crime')

title: First-order Analysis: Spatial Intensity
text:
Summary and Conclusions

What we did

Defined the intensity function \(\lambda(\mathbf{s})\) and contrasted quadrat (binned, test-oriented) and kernel (smooth, mapping-oriented) estimation.
Ran the quadrat-count test at \(8\times 8\) resolution: index of dispersion far above 1, and both the analytical and Monte Carlo tests reject CSR decisively: confirming Chapter 1.1’s visual impression.
Checked sensitivity to grid resolution and flagged where the chi-square approximation becomes unreliable (small expected counts), while noting the qualitative conclusion (overdispersion) is robust throughout.
Estimated a kernel intensity surface with the package’s uniform edge correction, and checked its integral against the known event count.
Compared Scott’s-rule and cross-validation bandwidths, and showed they disagree by roughly a factor of four here, in the direction theory predicts (CV undersmooths, Scott’s rule oversmooths).
Mapped relative risk for two crime types against the rest of crime, showing that “risk relative to the local baseline” is a different, and more actionable, map than raw density.



Practical takeaways

A significant quadrat test does not say where intensity is elevated, only that it is: kernel density is the complementary tool for that.
Bandwidth choice is not a detail: the same data can look like two dozen hot spots or two broad regions depending on \(h\) alone. Report the bandwidth, and show more than one.
A crime-type map that just reproduces the overall crime density map is not telling you anything new about that crime type: relative risk strips out the shared background.
None of this chapter’s methods use information about interaction between events (do assaults cluster near other assaults, beyond what the intensity surface predicts?): that is Chapter 1.3’s second-order question, logically separate from everything estimated here.



Next steps
Chapter 1.3 (Second-order and Distance-based Summary Functions) takes the interaction question head on: nearest-neighbour statistics, Ripley’s K and L, and the pair correlation function, all of which ask whether events are closer together (or farther apart) than their intensity alone would predict.

title: Module Map, Architecture, and Learning Paths
text:
Module Overview

Point Pattern Analysis

What it is: A set of event locations in a bounded study window; the locations themselves carry the information.
Core question: Are events clustered, dispersed, or consistent with Complete Spatial Randomness?
Dataset: Buffalo crime incidents 2018 (crime_data_2018.csv, buffalo_city.shp)
Library: geolattice.spatial_statistics.pointpattern








Notebook
Focus




04.01.1 Point Pattern Fundamentals
Point processes, observation windows, marks, and CSR as the null hypothesis


04.01.2 Spatial Intensity
First-order properties: raw intensity, KDE, bandwidth selection, covariate-adjusted intensity


04.01.3 Second-Order Functions
\(K(r)\), \(L(r)\), \(G(r)\), \(F(r)\), \(J(r)\): theory, estimation, clustered vs. regular patterns


04.01.4 Hypothesis Testing
Monte-Carlo envelopes, global and pointwise tests, multiple-testing corrections, power


04.01.5 Areal Integration & Pitfalls
Aggregating points to areal counts, edge effects, inhomogeneous extensions, MAUP



Key theory. A spatial point process \(\Phi\) is a random, locally finite set of points in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). The intensity \(\lambda(s)\) is the expected number of events per unit area near \(s\). Under CSR, \(\lambda(s) = \lambda\) (constant). The second-order intensity underpins Ripley’s \(K\)-function:
\[K(r) = \frac{1}{\lambda}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\text{events within distance }r\text{ of a typical event}\bigr]\]
Under CSR, \(K(r) = \pi r^2\). Values above signal clustering; values below signal regularity.


Spatial Autocorrelation

What it is: Lattice/areal data—one numeric value per polygon.
Core question: Is the spatial arrangement of values more similar (or dissimilar) than chance?
Dataset: US county diabetes prevalence, Northeast and Atlantic regions
Library: geolattice.spatial_statistics.weights, esda, viz








Notebook
Focus




04.02.1 Concepts, Data & Foundations
Tobler’s first law, dependence vs. heterogeneity, MAUP, dataset introduction


04.02.2 Spatial Weights
Contiguity (rook, queen), KNN, distance-band, row-standardisation, higher-order weights


04.02.3 Visualization & Exploratory Analysis
Choropleths, Moran scatterplot, spatial lag plots, quantile maps


04.02.4 Global Autocorrelation
Moran’s \(I\), Geary’s \(C\), Getis-Ord \(G\): permutation inference


04.02.5 Local Autocorrelation: LISA
Local Moran’s \(I_i\), Getis-Ord \(G_i^*\), LISA cluster maps


04.02.6 Sensitivity, Pitfalls & Exercises
Weight-choice sensitivity, boundary effects, MAUP revisited



Key theory. Moran’s \(I\):
\[I = \frac{n}{S_0}\cdot\frac{\sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}(z_i-\bar{z})(z_j-\bar{z})}{\sum_i(z_i-\bar{z})^2},\qquad S_0=\sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}\]
Under spatial randomness, \(\mathbb{E}[I] = -1/(n-1)\approx 0\). Local Moran \(I_i\) identifies HH, LL, HL, and LH clusters.


Spatial Regression

What it is: Regression that accounts for spatial autocorrelation in residuals or in the response.
Core question: What covariates drive a spatial outcome, and how do we obtain valid inference despite dependence?
Dataset: diabetes_atlantic.shp (666 counties)
Library: geolattice.spatial_statistics.regression








Notebook
Focus




04.03.1 Foundations
Why OLS fails; substantive vs. nuisance dependence; model taxonomy


04.03.2 OLS Baseline & Diagnostics
Moran \(I\) on residuals; LM-lag, LM-error, robust variants


04.03.3 Model Selection
LM decision tree; AIC/BIC; cross-validation


04.03.4 Model Families
SLM, SEM, SDM, SARAR, GNS; ML and GMM estimation


04.03.5 Comparison & Reporting
Marginal effects (direct/indirect/total); spatial multiplier


04.03.6 Limits & Connections
Endogeneity, panels, connections to GWR


04.03.7 Exercises
Structured exercises on the Atlantic dataset



Key theory. Spatial Lag (SLM/SAR): \(y = \rho W y + X\beta + \varepsilon\). Spatial Error (SEM): \(y = X\beta + u\), \(u = \lambda W u + \varepsilon\). SAR models substantive interaction; SEM models nuisance dependence. Lagrange Multiplier tests on OLS residuals guide the choice.


Spatial Cluster Analysis

What it is: Methods that locate statistically significant concentrations of high (or low) values.
Core question: Where are the hotspots, and are they statistically significant?
Dataset: diabetes_northeast.shp (217 counties)
Library: geolattice.spatial_statistics.cluster








Notebook
Focus




04.04.1 Concepts & Overview
Value clusters, location clusters, density clusters, spatial outliers


04.04.2 Hotspot Detection
Getis-Ord \(G_i^*\), local Moran, FDR corrections


04.04.3 Density & Location Clustering
DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, OPTICS on points and areal centroids


04.04.4 Scan Statistic
Kulldorff spatial scan (Poisson, Bernoulli); circular and flexible windows


04.04.5 Regionalisation
SKATER, REDCAP, WARD-spatial


04.04.6 Comparing & Validating
Silhouette, Calinski–Harabász, spatial compactness


04.04.7 Bridges
Hand-offs to regression (Part 3) and disease mapping (Part 5)


04.04.8 Exercises
Crime hotspots, epidemic clusters, zoning



Key theory. Kulldorff’s scan maximises a likelihood-ratio statistic over windows \(A\) and obtains \(p\)-values by Monte Carlo under the null—no asymptotic tables required.


Disease Mapping & Bayesian Smoothing

What it is: Small-area estimation that produces stable, uncertainty-aware disease rate maps.
Core question: How do we distinguish true spatial patterns from sampling noise in small-population areas?
Dataset: diabetes_northeast.shp (217 counties)
Library: geolattice.spatial_statistics.bayes








Notebook
Focus

Objectives, small-area problem, data prep, raw SMR estimates


04.05.5
Empirical Bayes (global Marshall; local Clayton–Kaldor)


04.05.6–04.05.7
BYM / ICAR models; MCMC (PyMC / NumPyro)


04.05.8–04.05.9
DIC/WAIC/LOO; shrinkage and exceedance maps


04.05.10–04.05.11
Reporting & ethics; handoffs and exercises



Key theory. BYM: \(y_i \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(E_i\exp(\alpha+\phi_i+\theta_i))\) with \(\phi\sim\operatorname{ICAR}(W,\sigma_\phi^2)\) (structured) and \(\theta_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_\theta^2)\) (unstructured).


Geographically Weighted Models

What it is: Locally calibrated regression and summaries whose coefficients vary in space.
Core question: Do relationships between variables change across the study region?
Dataset: diabetes_atlantic.shp (666 counties)
Library: geolattice.spatial_statistics.gwmodel








Notebook
Focus

Motivation, data, kernels & bandwidth selection


04.06.4–04.06.5

04.06.6–04.06.8
MGWR, GW-PCA; diagnostics; comparison with OLS/SAR


04.06.9–04.06.11
Spatial ML ensembles; GTWR; geographic deep models


04.06.12–04.06.14
Scaling; troubleshooting; exercises



Key theory. \(\hat{\beta}(s_i)=(X^\top W(s_i)X)^{-1}X^\top W(s_i)y\) with kernel weights decaying from \(s_i\). Bandwidth \(b\) trades local fidelity against noise; MGWR allows a separate \(b_k\) per covariate.


Spatial Interpolation

What it is: Prediction of a continuous field at unsampled locations.
Core question: What is the value at an unmeasured location, and how uncertain is that estimate?
Dataset: CA_pm25_2025.csv (163 California monitors)
Library: geolattice.spatial_statistics.interpolate








Notebook
Focus

Concepts; exploratory variogram and trend detection


04.07.3
Deterministic methods: IDW, RBF, natural neighbour


04.07.4–04.07.5
Variogram modelling; ordinary/universal kriging; validation


04.07.6–04.07.7
Regression kriging, co-kriging; areal / dasymetric interpolation


04.07.8
Exercises: PM2.5 reconstruction



Key theory. Ordinary kriging is a BLUP: \(\hat{Z}(s_0)=\sum_i\lambda_i Z(s_i)\) with \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), weights from the variogram system.


Spatial Sampling & Design

What it is: Selecting spatial samples that support valid, efficient inference.
Core question: Where should we place observations to minimise cost and maximise precision?
Dataset: diabetes_usa.csv (3,107 US counties as a known population laboratory)
Library: geolattice.spatial_statistics.sampling

Focus

Design-based vs. model-based inference; spatial balance


04.08.2
SRS, systematic, stratified, cluster, BAS, GRTS

Horvitz–Thompson estimation and design effect

Monitoring network design: add/drop optimisations


04.08.5
Exercises



Key theory. \(\hat{T}_{HT}=\sum_{i\in S} y_i/\pi_i\) is unbiased under any probability sample. Spatial balance (GRTS, BAS) reduces variance by exploiting positive autocorrelation.


Spatio-Temporal Analysis

What it is: Spatial methods extended to multiple time points—the space–time cube.
Core question: How do spatial patterns, clusters, and relationships evolve over time?
Dataset: County panel 1998–2012; Buffalo crime 2018
Library: geolattice.spatial_statistics.spacetime (builds on esda, cluster, gwmodel)








Notebook
Focus

Space–time cube; separable vs. non-separable structure


04.09.2
Space–time weights; space–time Moran \(I\)


04.09.3
Emerging hotspot analysis (Mann–Kendall + Getis-Ord)

Space–time KDE; Knox test; STDBSCAN

Space–time kriging; product-sum covariance

Key theory. Separability means \(\lambda(s,t)=\lambda_s(s)\cdot\lambda_t(t)\). The Knox statistic counts pairs that are close in both space and time and compares against time-permuted nulls.

title: Spatial Statistics
text:
What Is Spatial Statistics?
Spatial statistics studies phenomena that vary over geographic space with methods that incorporate location, proximity, and spatial structure. The discipline sits at the intersection of probability theory, geostatistics, econometrics, and computational geography.
Classical statistics asks: given a sample, what can we say about a population? Spatial statistics asks an additional question: given that the sample is arranged in space, how does that arrangement change what we can say? The answer is not cosmetic. When neighbouring counties share climate, policy, and demographics, their residuals are correlated; treating them as independent observations invents degrees of freedom that do not exist.

Four ways spatial data differ from classical data









Difference
Classical assumption
Spatial reality
Consequence of ignoring it




Dependence
Observations are independent
Nearby units share similar values
Inflated significance; biased coefficients when spillovers exist


Scale
The unit of analysis is given
Results change with aggregation level (MAUP)
Correlations and model fit that are artefacts of zoning


Support
All observations have the same geometric form
Points ≠ areas ≠ continuous fields
Wrong likelihood, wrong null, wrong visualisation


Null model
“No difference” or “zero slope”
Complete Spatial Randomness (homogeneous Poisson process)
Pattern declared significant (or not) against the wrong baseline





Working definition

Spatial statistics is the set of models, estimators, and tests in which location enters the likelihood, the covariance, or the sampling design, not merely the map legend.

That definition covers point processes (crime locations), lattice/areal models (county diabetes rates), geostatistical fields (PM2.5 at monitors), and space–time extensions of all three. It deliberately excludes pure cartography: a choropleth without a model is visualisation, not spatial statistics.

title: Spatial Statistics
text:
Why Spatial Statistics Matters
Ignoring spatial structure produces measurable harm. Four failure modes recur across applied work:

Inflated significance
Spatially autocorrelated residuals shrink estimated standard errors. A regression that reports \(p < 0.01\) under OLS may be non-significant once a spatial lag or spatial error term is included. Policy that reacts to false discoveries wastes resources and erodes trust.


Biased coefficients
When the dependence is substantive—one area’s outcome spills over into its neighbours—omitting that structure biases every coefficient, not just the standard errors. Housing prices, disease prevalence, and voting returns routinely exhibit this form of dependence.


Misleading maps
Raw small-area rates for rare events are dominated by sampling noise. A county of 2,000 people with two cancer cases looks like a crisis; a county of two million with the same rate looks unremarkable. Without empirical Bayes or hierarchical smoothing, maps point to spurious hotspots and drive wasteful allocation.


Missed heterogeneity
A single global coefficient can conceal the regions most in need of intervention. The effect of poverty on diabetes may be strong in rural counties and weak in dense metros. Geographically weighted and multiscale models exist precisely to recover that variation.


Application domains







Domain
Typical spatial question




Epidemiology / public health
Cluster detection, disease mapping, access to care


Criminology
Hotspot policing, patrol optimisation


Environmental science
Air/water quality interpolation, exposure assessment


Urban planning
Housing-price gradients, neighbourhood effects


Agriculture
Yield mapping, precision-fertiliser placement


Ecology
Species distribution models, habitat connectivity


Economics
Spatial spillovers, market-area definition


Climate science
Temperature/precipitation field reconstruction



If your data have coordinates, polygons, or monitoring locations, at least one of these questions is already on the table—whether or not the analysis has acknowledged it.

title: Spatial Statistics
text:
The Nine Driving Questions
Module 04 is organised around the questions practitioners actually ask. Each question maps to a Part, a data support, and a family of methods.








Question
Example
Part




Pattern — Are events clustered, dispersed, or random?
Is crime concentrated in specific city blocks?
Part 1 · Point Pattern Analysis


Dependence — Do nearby places share similar values?
Do counties with high diabetes rates border each other?
Part 2 · Spatial Autocorrelation


Process — What drives a spatially varying outcome?
Which socio-economic factors predict county-level disease?
Part 3 · Spatial Regression


Cluster — Where are statistically significant concentrations?

title: GeoLattice: Spatial Statistics
text:
Spatial statistics asks whether a pattern on a map is real. Are cases of a disease closer together than chance would put them? Are high values next to high values? Does a relationship hold everywhere, or change from place to place? Which counties are hot spots, and how stable is a rate based on a few hundred people? Each method in this chapter replaces a visual impression with a model, a test and a measure of uncertainty that respects the fact that nearby places are alike.
These 77 notebooks are chapter 04 of the GeoLattice tutorials. They cover point patterns, spatial autocorrelation, spatial regression, clustering, disease mapping, geographically weighted models, interpolation, sampling design and space-time analysis, and finish with five capstone projects, using geolattice.spatial_statistics with real data from the United States.

Every spatial test starts by saying who is a neighbour of whom. A spatial weights matrix records that: polygons that share an edge or a corner, the k nearest points, everything within a distance, or the edges of a graph. Spatial regression
Ordinary least squares assumes the errors are independent, which spatial data rarely allow. Diagnostics on the OLS residuals, especially the Lagrange multiplier tests, say whether the dependence belongs in the outcome (a spatial lag model) or in the errors (a spatial error model).

The Georgia data bundled with the package (159 county centroids) runs this whole workflow:
import geolattice.spatial_statistics as sstat
from geolattice.spatial_statistics.weights import KNN
from geolattice.spatial_statistics.esda import Moran, Moran_Local
from geolattice.spatial_statistics.regression import OLS, lm_tests, SpatialLag
from geolattice.spatial_statistics.gwmodel import GWR

georgia, predictors, response = sstat.datasets.load_georgia()   # 159 county centroids
w = KNN(georgia, k=6)                                             # 6 nearest counties

print(Moran(georgia["PctBach"], w, seed=0))                       # global autocorrelation
lisa = Moran_Local(georgia["PctBach"], w, seed=0)                 # local clusters (LISA)

X = georgia[["PctRural", "PctPov", "PctBlack"]]
ols = OLS(georgia["PctBach"], X, w=w)                             # baseline model
print(lm_tests(ols, w))                                           # lag or error?
print(SpatialLag(georgia["PctBach"], X, w))                       # spatial lag model
gwr = GWR().fit(X, georgia["PctBach"], georgia.geometry)          # local coefficients
