The location of peak density shifts modestly but noticeably across the four time-of-day slices, and the height of the peak also changes: the busiest slice’s hotspot is visibly more concentrated than the quietest one’s, not merely relocated. Both observations matter for the same reason Chapter 9.3’s Section 5 did: a single pooled density map (Section 3) would average all four of these patterns together, hiding exactly the time-varying structure this slicing approach reveals.

title: Space-Time Point Patterns and Density
section: Separable vs. Product Kernels: What Slicing Does Not Give You
text:
Separable vs. Product Kernels: What Slicing Does Not Give You
What Sections 4-5 actually did: four independent spatial KDE calls, each using only the subset of points falling in that time bin. This is, implicitly, the simplest possible separable space-time density model, it treats each time slice as its own self-contained spatial process, sharing no information at all across slices. It works, and it is honest about being an approximation, but it has two real limitations a genuine joint space-time KDE would address:

No smoothing across time. A slice with few points (the quietest quartile here) gets a noisier density estimate than a slice with many, purely because each slice is estimated in isolation. A joint estimator with a temporal kernel bandwidth would let nearby time bins share statistical strength, the same way a spatial kernel lets nearby locations share it.
No genuine space-time interaction surface. A true product kernel estimator, \(\hat{\lambda}(\mathbf{s}, t) = \sum_i K_s(\mathbf{s} - \mathbf{s}_i; h_s) \, K_t(t - t_i; h_t)\), evaluated on a continuous time axis rather than four discrete bins, would reveal whether the spatial bandwidth of clustering itself changes with time of day (a genuinely non-separable effect, in the Chapter 9.1 sense), something four independent snapshots, however finely sliced, can suggest visually but never formally test.

Building that estimator well: choosing a joint bandwidth, handling the edge correction Part 1’s kde already applies in space but would also need in time, and validating it against a real alternative: is real, unimplemented work. This chapter’s four-panel comparison is a legitimate, honest first look at whether time-of-day matters spatially at all (Section 5’s answer: yes, modestly); it is not a substitute for the fuller model the outline’s stub docstring gestures at.

title: Space-Time Point Patterns and Density
text:
Summary and Conclusions
This chapter used Part 1’s genuine spatial KDE four times, once per time-of-day slice, to approximate a space-time density picture the library does not yet estimate jointly.

What we did

Built one shared analysis window and a pooled full-day spatial density surface as a baseline.
Flagged that hour_of_day (1-12) is undocumented and possibly not a standard 24-hour clock: and that its 12 bucket has roughly double any other value’s count: before using it for anything.
Ran four independent pointpattern.kde calls, one per time-of-day quartile, on a shared window and colour scale.
Found both the location and the height of peak density shift across the day: evidence of genuine, time-varying spatial structure that a single pooled map would hide.
Explained precisely what Sections 4-5’s per-slice approach is (an implicitly separable model) and is not (a true product-kernel joint space-time estimator), and what building the latter honestly would require.



Practical takeaways

Slicing a spatial estimator across time bins is a legitimate, useful first look at space-time structure: but say so explicitly, and do not present it as a joint density estimate.
Always check an unfamiliar categorical time field’s actual value distribution before binning it: an unexplained imbalance (like hour_of_day=12’s double count here) can quietly bias which slice looks busiest.
A shared colour scale and a shared analysis window across slices are both required before any visual comparison between them means anything.



Next steps
Chapter 9.5 (Space-Time Interpolation) turns from point-pattern density to interpolating a continuous field across both space and time: and is, honestly, the chapter where this Part’s library gap is largest.

title: Regression with Space-Time Data
section: A Hand-Built Two-Way Fixed-Effects Panel Model
text:
A Hand-Built Two-Way Fixed-Effects Panel Model
Not a geolattice.spatial_statistics function. A standard two-way fixed-effects panel model removes every time-invariant county characteristic (rural vs. urban, historical industry, anything not in the covariate list) and every nationwide year-specific shock (a policy change, a recession) by demeaning: subtract each county’s own 15-year mean, subtract each year’s own national mean, add back the grand mean, then run OLS on what remains : purely the within-county, year-to-year co-movement between the covariates and RATE.


Code
cols = covariates + ["RATE"]
grand_mean = panel[cols].mean()
county_mean = panel.groupby("FIPS")[cols].transform("mean")
year_mean = panel.groupby("Year")[cols].transform("mean")
demeaned = panel[cols] - county_mean - year_mean + grand_mean

fe_model = OLS(demeaned["RATE"], demeaned[covariates])
print(fe_model.coef_frame().round(4))
print(f"\nwithin R2: {fe_model.r2:.4f}")

Why the Coefficients Flip: Between vs. Within Variation
Side by side, the two models tell strikingly different stories about the same covariates.

comparison = pd.DataFrame({

    "two-way FE (within)": fe_model.coef_frame().set_index("variable")["coef"],

PM25 and SO2 flip sign entirely between the two models: positive in pooled OLS, negative once county and year fixed effects are removed. This is a textbook illustration of between-vs-within confounding: pooled OLS’s PM25 coefficient reflects which counties tend to have both higher pollution and higher RATE: likely capturing unobserved, time-invariant regional characteristics correlated with both (industrial history, population density, baseline healthcare access) rather than a genuine causal effect of pollution itself. The fixed-effects estimate instead asks a much narrower, more defensible question: within the same county, in years when PM25 happened to be higher than that county’s own average, was RATE also higher or lower than that county’s own average? The within-county answer is negative: the opposite conclusion pooled OLS would suggest, and a direct demonstration of why panel data’s fixed-effects structure is not a minor technical refinement but can genuinely reverse a substantive conclusion.
SMOKING and POVERTY stay the same sign but shrink substantially (SMOKING: 2.49 to 0.19), while NO2 stays positive and similar in magnitude: not every covariate is equally confounded by omitted county-level characteristics.

title: Regression with Space-Time Data
section: GTWR: Fitting a Coefficient Surface Meant to Vary in Space and Time
text:
GTWR: Fitting a Coefficient Surface Meant to Vary in Space and Time
Part 6’s GTWR fits a coefficient surface that varies smoothly and locally across both space and time, neither pooled OLS’s “everywhere, always the same” nor fixed effects’ “one within-county average effect.” Following Part 6’s established resource-safe pattern: a modest county subset (Northeast, 217 counties) across a handful of years, n_jobs=2.

northeast = gpd.read_file(DATA / "diabetes_northeast.shp")

print(f"coef_ shape: {gtwr.coef_.shape}  (one row per space-time observation, "
     f"{gtwr.coef_.shape[1]} columns = intercept + {len(covariates)} covariates)")

GTWR, as just called with the constructor’s own documented example settings (lambda_=0.5), is not actually letting the temporal dimension affect the fit at all. Section 7 finds out exactly why.

title: Regression with Space-Time Data
section: A Real GTWR Bug: Two of Its Time Parameters Do Almost Nothing
text:
A Real GTWR Bug: Two of Its Time Parameters Do Almost Nothing
Part 6, Chapter 6.10 already found GTWR.predict() silently ignores its times argument for new predictions. What Section 6 just found is different and, in a sense, more serious: even the fitted, in-sample coefficients barely vary with time. Reading the source directly finds two separate causes.


Code
import inspect
print(inspect.getsource(GTWR.fit))


    def fit(self, X, y, geometry, times):
        """
        Calibrate GTWR.

        Parameters
        ----------
        X        : array-like (n, p)
        y        : array-like (n,)
        geometry : ndarray (n, 2) or GeoSeries
        times    : array-like (n,)   Temporal coordinates.
        """
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float).ravel()
        times = np.asarray(times, dtype=float).ravel()
        coords = _parse_geometry(geometry)

        n, p = X.shape
        X_int = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), X])
        self.coords_ = coords
        self.times_  = times
        self.X_ = X_int
        self.y_ = y

        # Optimise lambda if not provided
        lam = self.lambda_
        if lam is None:
            lam = self._select_lambda(X_int, y, coords, times)
        self.lambda_ = lam

        bw = self.bandwidth_s if self.bandwidth_s else 20
        self.bandwidth_ = float(bw)

        D_st = _st_distance(coords, times, lam)
        kernel = SpatialKernel(self.kernel, self.fixed, self.bandwidth_)

        results = parallel_map(
            (delayed(_fit_gtwr_point)(i, X_int, y, D_st, kernel)
             for i in range(n)),
            n_jobs=self.n_jobs,
        )

        self.coef_ = np.array([r["coef"] for r in results])
        self.fitted_ = np.array([r["fitted_i"] for r in results])
        self.residuals_ = y - self.fitted_
        hat_diag = np.array([r["hat_ii"] for r in results])
        self.effective_df_ = float(np.sum(hat_diag))
        rss = float(np.sum(self.residuals_ ** 2))
        self.aicc_ = aicc(rss, n, self.effective_df_)
        self.std_err_ = np.ones_like(self.coef_) * 0.1
        self.t_values_ = self.coef_ / 0.1
        self.p_values_ = t_to_p(self.t_values_, df=max(n - p - 1, 1))
        return self



bandwidth_t is stored in __init__ and never read again. It appears in the docstring, it is saved as self.bandwidth_t, and it is not referenced anywhere else in fit(), predict(), or any helper function, confirmed by searching the entire gwmodel package for the string bandwidth_t and finding only its docstring mention and its one assignment. Passing any value at all for bandwidth_t has zero effect on the fitted model.
The actual space-time distance comes entirely from lambda_, combined as \(d_{st} = \sqrt{d_s^2 + \lambda \, d_t^2}\) (visible in _st_distance, called inside fit() above): this part of the code does exist and does run. The problem is scale: \(d_t\) is measured in whatever units times is given in (here, literally the calendar year, so a difference of at most 8 across a 5-year subset), while \(d_s\) is measured in metres (here, ranging into the hundreds of thousands). At the class’s own documented example value, lambda_=0.5, the temporal term \(\sqrt{0.5}\times 8 \approx 5.7\) is utterly swamped by a spatial bandwidth of bandwidth_s=80 (already in the same units as \(d_s\)): the combined kernel weight barely distinguishes a same-county pair 8 years apart from a same-county pair in the same year, because 5.7 is a tiny fraction of an 80-unit bandwidth either way.


Code
one_fips_idx = sub.index[sub["FIPS"] == one_fips].tolist()
lambda_grid = [0.5, 1e3, 1e5, 1e7, 1e9]
rows = []
for lam in lambda_grid:
    m = GTWR(bandwidth_s=80, lambda_=lam, fixed=False, kernel="bisquare", n_jobs=2)
    m.fit(X_gtwr, y_gtwr, coords_gtwr, times_gtwr)
    coefs = m.coef_[[sub.index.get_loc(i) for i in one_fips_idx], 1]   # SMOKING column
    rows.append({"lambda_": lam, "SMOKING coef range across 5 years": coefs.max() - coefs.min()})

Confirmed directly: only once lambda_ is pushed to roughly \(10^5\)-\(10^9\): many orders of magnitude above the documented example’s 0.5: does the temporal dimension start to visibly move the fitted coefficients at all. Anyone following the class’s own docstring example on real year-and-metres data is, in practice, fitting a spatial-only GWR model and calling it GTWR without any warning. This is a genuine, verified bug: not a matter of taste in default settings, but a parameter (bandwidth_t) that is silently inert, and a second parameter (lambda_) whose usable range depends entirely on the ratio between the user’s spatial and temporal units: something neither the docstring nor the constructor signature discloses.
The honest workaround, if GTWR must be used today: rescale times into the same rough numeric range as the spatial coordinates before fitting (e.g., multiply year by an estimated “kilometres per year” the way Chapter 9.5’s hand-built space-time IDW did), and treat lambda_=0.5 as meaningless unless that rescaling has been done first: never trust the constructor’s own example value at face value.

title: Regression with Space-Time Data
section: Computing R2 Without the Broken score
text:
Computing R2 Without the Broken score
Chapter 6.10 also found GTWR.score()/predict() ignore times for new predictions. Confirmed again here, briefly, before computing this chapter’s own \(R^2\) honestly.


Code
print(inspect.getsource(gtwr.score))


    def score(self, X, y, geometry) -> float:
        """Return default goodness-of-fit score (R² for regression)."""
        yhat = self.predict(X, geometry)
        y = np.asarray(y)
        ss_res = np.sum((y - yhat) ** 2)
        ss_tot = np.sum((y - y.mean()) ** 2)
        return 1.0 - ss_res / max(ss_tot, 1e-10)



score() calls self.predict(X, geometry): not even passing times. The fix is the same one Chapter 6.10 used: bypass score()/predict() and compute \(R^2\) directly from the already-fitted coef_ array, which is the exact local coefficient vector used to fit each space-time observation.


Code
X_design = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X_gtwr)), X_gtwr])
y_fitted = np.sum(X_design * gtwr.coef_, axis=1)
ss_res = np.sum((y_gtwr - y_fitted) ** 2)
ss_tot = np.sum((y_gtwr - y_gtwr.mean()) ** 2)
r2_gtwr = 1 - ss_res / ss_tot
print(f"GTWR in-sample R2 (computed from coef_ directly, bypassing the broken score()): {r2_gtwr:.4f}")
print("(fit with lambda_=0.5 -- i.e., functionally a spatial-only GWR fit, per Section 7's finding)")


GTWR in-sample R2 (computed from coef_ directly, bypassing the broken score()): 0.8347
(fit with lambda_=0.5 -- i.e., functionally a spatial-only GWR fit, per Section 7's finding)

GTWR’s in-sample \(R^2\) is the highest: but, per Section 7’s finding, at lambda_=0.5 this fit is functionally a spatial-only GWR model fit once per county, not a genuinely space-time-varying one; its advantage over pooled OLS reflects local spatial flexibility (Part 6’s whole GWR story), not anything meaningfully time-varying. The real question these three models answer differently is not “which fits best” but “what kind of relationship am I even claiming exists”: one fixed national relationship (pooled OLS), a single average within-county effect purged of place-and-time confounding (fixed effects), or: in principle, though not as delivered by this library today at documented default settings: one that varies smoothly across both space and time (GTWR). Section 5’s sign flip is the finding most worth taking away from this chapter’s working results; Section 7’s bug report is the one most worth remembering before reaching for GTWR again.

title: Regression with Space-Time Data
text:
Summary and Conclusions
This chapter closed this Part’s regression content by fitting the same national panel three genuinely different ways: and, in the process, found a second real bug in GTWR, beyond the one Chapter 6.10 already documented.

What we did

Fit pooled OLS on the full 46,605-row panel: one relationship, nationwide, always.
Hand-built a two-way fixed-effects panel model via county- and year-demeaning (no geolattice.spatial_statistics panel regression exists) and found PM25 and SO2 flip sign entirely compared to pooled OLS: a genuine between-vs-within confounding effect, not a minor technical correction.
Fit GTWR on a Northeast subset at its own documented example settings (lambda_=0.5) and found the fitted SMOKING coefficient for any single county is identical, to 6+ decimal places, across all five of its observed years: the temporal dimension has essentially no effect on the fit.
Traced this to a genuine bug with two parts: bandwidth_t is stored but never read anywhere in the codebase, and lambda_’s usable range depends entirely on the (undocumented) ratio between the user’s spatial and temporal coordinate units: at the class’s own example value, that range is nowhere close to large enough for real year-and-metres data, confirmed by needing lambda_ in the \(10^5\)-\(10^9\) range before the temporal dimension visibly moved any coefficient.
Reconfirmed Chapter 6.10’s separate predict()/score() time-blindness bug, and again computed \(R^2\) from the already-fitted coef_ array as the honest workaround.
Compared all three models’ fit, while explaining why “highest \(R^2\)” is the wrong way to read that comparison given Section 7’s finding about what that fit actually represents.



Practical takeaways

Always check whether a coefficient’s sign is driven by which units differ (between variation) or by how units change over time (within variation) before trusting a pooled panel regression’s coefficient as causal: Section 5’s PM25/SO2 flip is the clearest possible illustration of why this matters.
A hand-built fixed-effects model is straightforward to construct from any OLS implementation via demeaning, no dedicated panel-regression class is required to do this correctly.
Never trust GTWR’s documented lambda_=0.5 example on real data without first checking whether your spatial and temporal coordinates are on comparable numeric scales: rescale time to match, or verify the temporal dimension is actually affecting fitted coefficients (Section 6’s single-county check) before reporting any GTWR result as space-time-varying.
Never call GTWR.score() expecting it to account for the time dimension; compute \(R^2\) from coef_ directly when an accurate in-sample fit statistic is needed.



This closes the library-supported/hand-built content for Part 9
Chapter 9.7 (Exercises) closes out the whole Part with two hands-on tasks drawn directly from Chapters 9.2 and 9.3’s findings.

title: Capstone: Presidential Voting Patterns, 2020 vs 2024 - Persistence and Shift
text:
Overview

Across contiguous-US counties, how much of the 2024 Republican vote geography was already present in 2020? Where did the two-party vote move between the two elections, does the move form spatial clusters, and which county characteristics (rurality, race/ethnicity, age, education, unemployment, poverty, population change, evangelical adherence) are associated with the level of support versus the change in support?

section: Data: the USA Health Data Atlas database
text:
Data: the USA Health Data Atlas database
The Atlas publishes its county data as JavaScript bundles. data_processing.py (in this folder) creates the SQLite schema and dataset catalog and then calls build_database.py, which downloads the bundles and parses each one into normalized tables:







Table
Content used here

One row per county × year (2004–2024): votes, shares, margin, source


county_indicators
Long table (dataset_id, fips, year, variable, value, unit) for Census PEP, CHR, SVI, Religion Census


dataset_catalog, data_load_log, source_records
Provenance: dataset descriptions, import status, each bundle’s metadata



If the database is empty, build it once (internet required, about 1 minute):

SQL extract: one row per county with both elections
The election table is long (county × year). We pivot it to wide in SQL so that each county carries its 2020 and 2024 counts side by side. Covariates come from county_indicators in a second query. Each (dataset, variable, year) triple in COVAR_SPEC becomes one column, with a few unit conversions:

CHR and SVI proportions (0–1) become percentages.
The Religion Census rate per 1,000 residents becomes per 100, capped at 100. Adherent counts above a county’s population are a known artifact of the Religion Census in small counties.
Population change is computed from the 2020 and 2023 PEP totals.

A county that the Religion Census covered (it has a total-adherents rate) but that reports no evangelical bodies gets 0 evangelical adherents, not a missing value. These are mostly small Plains and Mountain counties dominated by Catholic or LDS congregations. If a county is absent from the 2020 census entirely, its 2010 value is used.


Code
ELECTION_SQL = """
SELECT fips,
       MAX(county_name)                                  AS county_name,
       MAX(state_name)                                   AS state_abbr,
       MAX(CASE WHEN year = 2020 THEN rep_votes   END)   AS rep_2020,
       MAX(CASE WHEN year = 2020 THEN dem_votes   END)   AS dem_2020,
       MAX(CASE WHEN year = 2020 THEN total_votes END)   AS tot_2020,
       MAX(CASE WHEN year = 2024 THEN rep_votes   END)   AS rep_2024,
       MAX(CASE WHEN year = 2024 THEN dem_votes   END)   AS dem_2024,
       MAX(CASE WHEN year = 2024 THEN total_votes END)   AS tot_2024
FROM presidential_election_results
WHERE year IN (2020, 2024)
GROUP BY fips
"""
votes = pd.read_sql(ELECTION_SQL, con)

# One query for every (dataset, variable, year) the covariates need.
wanted = set()
for dataset, variable, year in COVAR_SPEC.values():
    for yr in (year if isinstance(year, tuple) else (year,)):
        wanted.add((dataset, variable, yr))
for yr in (2010, 2020):                                         # evangelical gap rules (see markdown)
    wanted.add(("religion_census", "dom_evan_rate", yr))
    wanted.add(("religion_census", "tot_rate", yr))
clauses = " OR ".join(["(d.dataset_name = ? AND i.variable = ? AND i.year = ?)"] * len(wanted))
INDICATOR_SQL = f"""
SELECT i.fips, d.dataset_name, i.variable, i.year, i.value
FROM county_indicators AS i
JOIN dataset_catalog  AS d USING (dataset_id)
WHERE {clauses}
"""
params = [p for triple in sorted(wanted) for p in triple]
long = pd.read_sql(INDICATOR_SQL, con, params=params)
wide = long.pivot_table(index="fips", columns=["dataset_name", "variable", "year"], values="value")
con.close()

covs = pd.DataFrame(index=wide.index)
for name, (dataset, variable, year) in COVAR_SPEC.items():
    if name == "pop_change":
        y0, y1 = year
        covs[name] = 100 * (wide[(dataset, variable, y1)] / wide[(dataset, variable, y0)] - 1)
    elif name == "pct_evangelical":
        # A county the census covered (tot_rate present) but with no evangelical bodies has 0 adherents.
        evan = {yr: wide[(dataset, variable, yr)].where(
                    wide[(dataset, variable, yr)].notna() | wide[(dataset, "tot_rate", yr)].isna(), 0.0)
                for yr in (2010, 2020)}
        covs[name] = (evan[2020].fillna(evan[2010]) / 10).clip(upper=100)
    elif dataset in ("county_health_rankings", "social_vulnerability_index"):
        covs[name] = 100 * wide[(dataset, variable, year)]
    else:
        covs[name] = wide[(dataset, variable, year)]
covs = covs.reset_index()

# Outcomes: GOP two-party shares and the shift between them.
votes["rep2p_2020"] = 100 * votes["rep_2020"] / (votes["rep_2020"] + votes["dem_2020"])
votes["rep2p_2024"] = 100 * votes["rep_2024"] / (votes["rep_2024"] + votes["dem_2024"])
votes["shift"] = votes["rep2p_2024"] - votes["rep2p_2020"]
votes["turnout_ratio"] = votes["tot_2024"] / votes["tot_2020"]

table = votes.merge(covs, on="fips", how="left")
display(Markdown(
    f"SQL returned **{len(votes)}** counties with at least one of the two elections and "
    f"**{len(long):,}** indicator values for **{len(covs)}** counties."
))
display(table[["fips", "county_name", "state_abbr", "rep2p_2020", "rep2p_2024", "shift", *COVARS]].head().round(2))

Join to county polygons, data-quality rules, and CRS audit

Zero-pad shapefile FIPS to five characters and inner-join to the SQL table.
Coverage rule. A county needs both elections and every covariate. This removes Connecticut, whose 2024 planning regions don’t match its 2020 counties.
Comparability rule. Flag counties whose 2024 ballot total is under ⅔ or over 1.5× the 2020 total. A jump that large usually means the two sources drew the county’s boundary differently. Jackson County, MO is the textbook case: MEDSL reports Kansas City separately in 2020, while the 2024 feed folds it into the county.
Audit the CRS and geometry, and keep the layer in metres (EPSG:5070).

Analysis coordinates are polygon centroids of the projected geometry.


Code
def crs_audit(gdf, name="layer"):
    """Return a DataFrame of data-quality checks for a GeoDataFrame."""
    rows = []
    add = lambda check, status, detail: rows.append({"check": check, "status": status, "detail": detail})
    crs = gdf.crs
    if crs is None:
        add("CRS declared", "FAIL", "no CRS: cannot reproject and units are unknown")
    else:
        add("CRS declared", "ok", crs.name)
        unit = crs.axis_info[0].unit_name
        add(
            "metric projected CRS",
            "ok" if crs.is_projected and unit == "metre" else "warn",
            f"{'geographic' if crs.is_geographic else 'projected'}, unit = {unit}",
        )
        if crs.area_of_use is not None:
            pts = gdf.geometry.representative_point()
            if crs.is_geographic:
                lon, lat = pts.x.to_numpy(), pts.y.to_numpy()
            else:
                lon, lat = Transformer.from_crs(crs, 4326, always_xy=True).transform(
                    pts.x.to_numpy(), pts.y.to_numpy()
                )
            w, s, e, n = crs.area_of_use.bounds
            in_lon = (lon >= w) & (lon <= e) if w <= e else (lon >= w) | (lon <= e)
            frac = float(np.mean(in_lon & (lat >= s) & (lat <= n)))
            add("inside the CRS's area of use", "ok" if frac > 0.99 else "FAIL",
                f"{100 * frac:.0f}% of features")
    bad = int((~gdf.geometry.is_valid).sum())
    empty = int(gdf.geometry.is_empty.sum())
    miss = int(gdf.geometry.isna().sum())
    add("valid, non-empty geometries", "ok" if bad + empty + miss == 0 else "warn",
        f"{bad} invalid, {empty} empty, {miss} missing")
    types = gdf.geom_type.value_counts().to_dict()
    add("geometry types", "ok" if len(types) == 1 else "note", str(types))
    add("unique index", "ok" if gdf.index.is_unique else "warn",
        f"{int(gdf.index.duplicated().sum())} duplicated index labels")
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("check")


shp = gpd.read_file(DATA / "US_COUNTY.shp")
shp["fips"] = shp["FIPS"].astype(int).astype(str).str.zfill(5)
merged = shp[["fips", "STATE", "COUNTY", "geometry"]].merge(table, on="fips", how="inner")
n_shp, n_join = len(shp), len(merged)

# Rule 2: both elections and all covariates present.
need = ["rep2p_2020", "rep2p_2024", *COVARS]
missing = merged[need].isna().any(axis=1)
# Rule 3: ballot totals comparable between the two sources.
not_comparable = ~missing & ~merged["turnout_ratio"].between(2 / 3, 1.5)

dropped = pd.concat([
    merged.loc[missing, ["fips", "COUNTY", "STATE"]].assign(reason="missing election year or covariate"),
    merged.loc[not_comparable, ["fips", "COUNTY", "STATE", "turnout_ratio", "shift"]]
          .assign(reason="2024/2020 ballot ratio outside [0.67, 1.5]"),
])
merged = merged.loc[~missing & ~not_comparable].copy()
merged = merged.set_crs(5070, allow_override=True)        # NAD83 Conus Albers (metres)

audit = crs_audit(merged)
audit.loc["FIPS join"] = ("ok", f"shp={n_shp}, joined={n_join}, kept={len(merged)}, dropped={len(dropped)}")

study = SpatialData(merged, y="shift", X=COVARS + ["rep2p_2020", "rep2p_2024"])
counties = study.gdf.reset_index(drop=True)
centroids = counties.geometry.centroid
coords = np.column_stack([centroids.x.to_numpy(), centroids.y.to_numpy()])

display(audit)
display(dropped.round(3))
display(Markdown(
    f"**{len(counties)}** counties remain (geometry **{study.geometry_type}**, CRS **EPSG:{counties.crs.to_epsg()}**). "

title: Capstone: Presidential Voting Patterns, 2020 vs 2024 - Persistence and Shift
section: Persistence vs Change at a Glance
text:
Persistence vs Change at a Glance
First the Republican two-party share in 2020, the same share in 2024, and their difference (shift = 2024 − 2020), all on one row. The Democratic share is just the complement of the Republican share, so it is not plotted separately.
The 2020 and 2024 maps should look almost the same — that is the persistence finding, not a plotting bug. County shares correlate at about r = 0.995, so a 20–80 % colour scale cannot show the 1–3 point moves. The third panel uses a tight diverging scale so those small moves become visible.


Code
# Democratic two-party share is the complement of the GOP two-party share.
counties["dem2p_2020"] = 100 - counties["rep2p_2020"]
counties["dem2p_2024"] = 100 - counties["rep2p_2024"]

# Sanity check: prove the year columns are not identical.
y20 = counties["rep2p_2020"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
y24 = counties["rep2p_2024"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
diff = y24 - y20
print(
    f"rep2p_2020 vs rep2p_2024:  "
    f"identical counties = {(diff == 0).sum()} / {len(diff)},  "
    f"mean |diff| = {np.mean(np.abs(diff)):.2f} pp,  "
    f"max |diff| = {np.max(np.abs(diff)):.2f} pp,  "
    f"r = {np.corrcoef(y20, y24)[0, 1]:.4f}"
)

# Three panels: 2020 level, 2024 level, and the difference that the level maps hide.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 5))

# Left / middle: same 20–80 % scale so the years are comparable.
for ax, col, title in [
    (axes[0], "rep2p_2020", "2020 Republican two-party share"),
    (axes[1], "rep2p_2024", "2024 Republican two-party share"),
]:
    counties.plot(
        column=col,
        cmap="Reds",
        vmin=20, vmax=80,
        legend=True,
        ax=ax,
        edgecolor="none",
        legend_kwds={"label": "Republican two-party share (%)", "shrink": 0.6},
    )
    ax.set_axis_off()
    ax.set_title(title)

# Right: same quantity as counties["shift"], on a tight diverging scale.
lim = float(np.nanpercentile(np.abs(diff), 99))
counties.plot(
    column="shift",
    cmap="RdBu_r",                                          # red = toward GOP, blue = toward Democrats
    norm=TwoSlopeNorm(vmin=-lim, vcenter=0, vmax=lim),      # white = no change
    legend=True,
    ax=axes[2],
    edgecolor="none",
    legend_kwds={"label": "GOP two-party shift (pp)", "shrink": 0.6},
)
axes[2].set_axis_off()
axes[2].set_title("Difference: 2024 − 2020")

fig.suptitle(
    "Republican two-party share by county — levels look alike; the shift does not",
    fontsize=13, fontweight="bold",
)
plt.tight_layout()

Covariate maps and collinearity
The nine baseline covariates, then variance-inflation factors (VIF). A VIF above about 5 would warn that two covariates carry nearly the same information, which inflates the uncertainty of their coefficients in OLS and GWR.


Code
# 3 × 3 grid: one panel per covariate.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(14, 11))
for ax, col in zip(axes.ravel(), COVARS):
    vals = counties[col]
    counties.plot(
        column=col,                                  # covariate to map
        cmap="YlGnBu",                               # sequential palette (low → high)
        vmin=vals.quantile(0.02),                    # clip 2 % tails so outliers don't wash out the map
        vmax=vals.quantile(0.98),
        legend=True, ax=ax, edgecolor="none",
        legend_kwds={"shrink": 0.55, "orientation": "horizontal", "pad": 0.02},
    )
    ax.set_axis_off()
    ax.set_title(COVAR_LABELS[col])
plt.suptitle("Baseline county covariates (Atlas database)", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout()
# ALT: Nine CONUS choropleths of rural share, Hispanic share, non-Hispanic Black share, age 65+, some college, unemployment, poverty percentile, population change 2020-23, and evangelical Protestant adherence.
plt.show()

# Standardise covariates once; every model below uses these z-scores so slopes are comparable.
X_raw = counties[COVARS].to_numpy(dtype=float)
X = (X_raw - X_raw.mean(axis=0)) / X_raw.std(axis=0)


def vif(Z):
    """Variance-inflation factor of each column of Z (regress it on the others)."""
    out = []
    for j in range(Z.shape[1]):
        others = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Z)), np.delete(Z, j, axis=1)])
        beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(others, Z[:, j], rcond=None)
        resid = Z[:, j] - others @ beta
        r2 = 1 - resid.var() / Z[:, j].var()
        out.append(1 / (1 - r2))
    return np.array(out)

text:
Weights, Sensitivity, and Islands
Queen contiguity is the default graph for county polygons. Counties with no Queen neighbour are linked to their nearest non-island county. We then check that Moran’s I for each outcome is stable across KNN graphs before committing to Queen.


Code
def attach_islands(w, xy):
    """Link each island to its nearest non-island county, both ways, then row-standardise."""
    ids = list(w.id_order)
    pos = {i: k for k, i in enumerate(ids)}
    islands = set(w.islands())
    neighbors = {i: list(w.neighbors[i]) for i in ids}
    if not islands:
        return W(neighbors, ids=ids, transform="row")
    tree = cKDTree(xy)
    for isl in islands:
        _, idxs = tree.query(xy[pos[isl]], k=min(25, len(ids)))
        for j in np.atleast_1d(idxs):
            other = ids[int(j)]
            if other == isl or other in islands:
                continue
            if other not in neighbors[isl]:
                neighbors[isl].append(other)
            if isl not in neighbors[other]:
                neighbors[other].append(isl)
            break
    return W(neighbors, ids=ids, transform="row")


w_raw = Queen(counties, transform="row")
w = attach_islands(w_raw, coords)
print("Queen (islands linked)")
print(w.summary())

graphs = {"Queen (linked)": w, **{f"KNN k={k}": KNN(counties, k=k, transform="row") for k in (4, 8, 12)}}
sens = pd.DataFrame({
    gname: {OUTCOMES[o]: Moran(counties[o].to_numpy(float), g, permutations=PERM, seed=SEED).I for o in OUTCOMES}
    for gname, g in graphs.items()
})
display(sens.round(3))

    f"in **{w.n_components()}** component(s). Across the four graphs Moran's I varies by at most "
    f"**{(sens.max(axis=1) - sens.min(axis=1)).max():.3f}** for any outcome, so the rest of the study uses **linked Queen**."
))

Global Autocorrelation: Is the Shift as Spatial as the Level?
Two-party share is strongly clustered in both years. title: Capstone: Presidential Voting Patterns, 2020 vs 2024 - Persistence and Shift
text:
Explanation: Same Covariates, Three Outcomes
We fit the same OLS with standardised covariates to 2020 share, 2024 share, and the shift. Because the covariates are z-scores, each coefficient is “percentage points per one-SD difference across counties”:

A covariate with almost the same slope in 2020 and 2024 marks a persistent association.
A covariate that matters for the shift but barely changes the level marks an association specific to 2024.

A fourth model adds 2020 share to the shift equation. Counties already near 80 % GOP have little room to move, so this separates ceiling effects from covariate effects.


Code
y_vec = {o: counties[o].to_numpy(dtype=float) for o in OUTCOMES}
ols = {o: OLS(y_vec[o], X, w=w, y_name=o, names=COVARS) for o in OUTCOMES}

z20 = ((y20 - y20.mean()) / y20.std()).reshape(-1, 1)
ols_cond = OLS(dy, np.hstack([X, z20]), w=w, y_name="shift", names=COVARS + ["rep2p_2020"])


def coef_series(model):
    cf = model.coef_frame().set_index("variable")
    return cf["coef"], cf["p_value"]


coef_tbl = pd.DataFrame({OUTCOMES[o]: coef_series(m)[0] for o, m in ols.items()})
coef_tbl["Shift | 2020 share"] = coef_series(ols_cond)[0]
pval_tbl = pd.DataFrame({OUTCOMES[o]: coef_series(m)[1] for o, m in ols.items()})
pval_tbl["Shift | 2020 share"] = coef_series(ols_cond)[1]
coef_tbl.loc["R²"] = [ols[o].r2 for o in OUTCOMES] + [ols_cond.r2]
display(coef_tbl.round(3))

# Coefficient comparison plot: 2020 vs 2024 slopes (left), shift slopes (right).

labels = [COVAR_LABELS[c] for c in COVARS]

             color="#fcae91", label="2020")

Spatial dependence in the residuals: LM tests, SLM, and SEM
Each OLS above ignores neighbours. Lagrange-multiplier tests on its residuals recommend a spatial lag (SLM) or spatial error (SEM) model. We fit both for every outcome and keep the lower AIC.

section: Heterogeneity: Where Do the Shift Associations Change Sign?
text:
Heterogeneity: Where Do the Shift Associations Change Sign?
A single national slope for Hispanic share or poverty can hide regional differences. Adaptive GWR estimates a local slope at every county. We choose the neighbour count \(k\) by AICc on a coarse grid and map all nine local slopes for the shift.
Then we refit GWR at the same \(k\) for 2020 and for 2024 and compare the local Hispanic-share slope between the two years. Where that slope rose, the Hispanic–Republican association changed in 2024.


Code
gwr_rows, gwr_fits = [], {}
for k in (100, 200, 400):                       # coarse adaptive-bandwidth grid (each fit ≈ 1 min)
    fit = GWR(bandwidth=k, fixed=False, kernel="bisquare", criterion="AICc", hat_matrix=True, n_jobs=-1)
    fit.fit(X, dy, coords)
    gwr_fits[k] = fit
    gwr_rows.append({"k": k, "aicc": fit.aicc_, "rmse": float(np.sqrt(np.mean(fit.residuals_ ** 2)))})
gwr_grid = pd.DataFrame(gwr_rows).sort_values("aicc").reset_index(drop=True)
display(gwr_grid.round(2))
best_k = int(gwr_grid.loc[0, "k"])
gwr = gwr_fits[best_k]

for j, col in enumerate(COVARS):                # column 0 of coef_ is the intercept

title: Capstone: Presidential Voting Patterns, 2020 vs 2024 - Persistence and Shift
section: Was the Shift Real? A Count Model Against a “Kept-2020” Expectation
text:
Was the Shift Real? A Count Model Against a “Kept-2020” Expectation
A 3-point shift in a county with 300 ballots is not the same evidence as a 3-point shift in one with 300,000. We treat 2024 Republican votes as counts and set the expectation to the votes the county would have cast if it had kept its 2020 two-party share:
\[E_i = \frac{\text{rep2p}_{2020,i}}{100}\,(\text{Rep}_{2024,i} + \text{Dem}_{2024,i}).\]

SMR = observed / expected. Values above 1 mean the county moved toward the GOP.
Empirical Bayes shrinks unstable small-county SMRs toward the national ratio.
BYM adds a spatial CAR effect and gives each county a posterior probability that it really moved right, \(P(\theta_i > 1)\).

This is not a turnout or persuasion model. It is a precision-aware map of the shift.


Code
observed = counties["rep_2024"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
expected = (y20 / 100) * ballots
raw_smr = smr(observed, expected)
eb = eb_gamma_poisson(observed, expected, method="mle", alpha=ALPHA)
bym = BYM(observed, expected, w, backend="gibbs", draws=400, tune=400, chains=2, thin=5, seed=SEED, alpha=ALPHA)

counties["smr"] = raw_smr
counties["eb"] = eb.estimate
counties["rr"] = bym.rr_mean
counties["p_right"] = bym.exceedance(1.0)

display(pd.DataFrame({"SMR": raw_smr, "EB": eb.estimate, "BYM": bym.rr_mean})
        .agg(["mean", "std", "min", "max"]).T.round(4))
display(bym.diagnostics.round(3))
small = ballots <= np.quantile(ballots, 0.2)
display(Markdown(
    f"National SMR (sum observed / sum expected) = **{observed.sum() / expected.sum():.4f}**. "
    f"SMR SD **{raw_smr.std():.4f}** becomes **{eb.estimate.std():.4f}** after EB and **{bym.rr_mean.std():.4f}** after BYM. "
    f"In the smallest fifth of counties the mean EB weight on the county's own data is **{eb.shrinkage[small].mean():.2f}** "
    f"against **{eb.shrinkage[~small].mean():.2f}** elsewhere. "
    f"**{(counties['p_right'] > 0.95).sum()}** of {len(counties)} counties have P(θ > 1) > 0.95 (a credible rightward move) and "
    f"**{(counties['p_right'] < 0.05).sum()}** have P(θ > 1) < 0.05 (a credible leftward move). "
    f"BYM max R-hat **{bym.max_rhat:.3f}**, min ESS **{bym.min_ess:.0f}**."
))

title: Capstone: Presidential Voting Patterns, 2020 vs 2024 - Persistence and Shift
text:
Machine-Learning Cross-Check: XGBoost and TreeSHAP
The guideline suggests a random-forest/XGBoost model with SHAP explanations. Gradient-boosted trees can find non-linearities and interactions that OLS cannot, such as Hispanic share mattering more in poorer counties. Two choices keep the comparison honest:

Spatial cross-validation. Folds are grouped by state, so the model is always scored on states it has never seen. Random folds would leak neighbouring counties between training and test sets.
TreeSHAP. XGBoost’s built-in pred_contribs=True returns per-county additive attributions with no extra package.



Code
import xgboost as xgb
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold

params = dict(n_estimators=400, max_depth=4, learning_rate=0.05, subsample=0.8,
              colsample_bytree=0.8, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1)
groups = counties["STATE"].to_numpy()
oof = np.full(len(dy), np.nan)
for train, test in GroupKFold(n_splits=8).split(X_raw, dy, groups):     # whole states held out
    model = xgb.XGBRegressor(**params).fit(X_raw[train], dy[train])
    oof[test] = model.predict(X_raw[test])

ss_res = np.sum((dy - oof) ** 2)
r2_cv = 1 - ss_res / np.sum((dy - dy.mean()) ** 2)

# OLS scored the same way (state-grouped folds) for a like-for-like comparison.
oof_ols = np.full(len(dy), np.nan)
for train, test in GroupKFold(n_splits=8).split(X_raw, dy, groups):
    A = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(train)), X_raw[train]])
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, dy[train], rcond=None)
    oof_ols[test] = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(test)), X_raw[test]]) @ beta
r2_cv_ols = 1 - np.sum((dy - oof_ols) ** 2) / np.sum((dy - dy.mean()) ** 2)

# Final model on all counties, then TreeSHAP contributions (last column = bias term).
xgb_model = xgb.XGBRegressor(**params).fit(X_raw, dy)
shap_vals = xgb_model.get_booster().predict(xgb.DMatrix(X_raw), pred_contribs=True)[:, :-1]
shap_imp = pd.Series(np.abs(shap_vals).mean(axis=0), index=[COVAR_LABELS[c] for c in COVARS]).sort_values()
for j, col in enumerate(COVARS):
    counties[f"shap_{col}"] = shap_vals[:, j]

# Spatial dependence the trees leave behind.
resid_ml = dy - oof
moran_ml = Moran(resid_ml, w, permutations=PERM, seed=SEED)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.4]})
axes[0].barh(shap_imp.index, shap_imp.values, color=COLORS["purple"])
axes[0].set_xlabel("mean |SHAP| (pp of shift)")
axes[0].set_title("XGBoost feature importance for the shift")
top_feat = COVARS[int(np.argmax(np.abs(shap_vals).mean(axis=0)))]
lim = float(np.nanpercentile(np.abs(counties[f"shap_{top_feat}"]), 98))
counties.plot(column=f"shap_{top_feat}", cmap="RdBu_r", norm=TwoSlopeNorm(vmin=-lim, vcenter=0, vmax=lim),
              legend=True, ax=axes[1], edgecolor="none", legend_kwds={"shrink": 0.6, "label": "SHAP (pp)"})
axes[1].set_axis_off()
axes[1].set_title(f"Where {COVAR_LABELS[top_feat]} pushed the predicted shift")
plt.tight_layout()
# ALT: Left, bar chart of mean absolute SHAP values for the nine covariates predicting the GOP shift; right, CONUS map of the SHAP contribution of the top covariate.
plt.show()

shap_top3 = ", ".join(f"**{lab}**" for lab in shap_imp.index[::-1][:3])
if top_feat == lead:
    rank_sentence = "Its top feature matches the lead covariate of the OLS shift model."
else:
    rank_sentence = (f"OLS ranks **{COVAR_LABELS[lead]}** first instead. A linear slope and a tree attribution "
                     f"share credit differently between correlated covariates, so read the two rankings together.")
display(Markdown(
    f"State-held-out R²: XGBoost **{r2_cv:.2f}** vs OLS **{r2_cv_ols:.2f}**. "
    f"TreeSHAP ranks {shap_top3} highest. {rank_sentence} "
    f"Out-of-fold residuals still have Moran's I = **{moran_ml.I:.3f}** (p = {moran_ml.p_value:.3f}). "
    f"Even a flexible non-spatial learner leaves regionally shared structure in the shift, which is the case "
    f"for the spatial models above."
))









State-held-out R²: XGBoost 0.36 vs OLS 0.26. TreeSHAP ranks % non-Hispanic Black, % Hispanic, Poverty <150% FPL (percentile) highest. OLS ranks % Hispanic first instead. A linear slope and a tree attribution share credit differently between correlated covariates, so read the two rankings together. Out-of-fold residuals still have Moran’s I = 0.356 (p = 0.001). Even a flexible non-spatial learner leaves regionally shared structure in the shift, which is the case for the spatial models above.

title: Capstone: Presidential Voting Patterns, 2020 vs 2024 - Persistence and Shift
text:
Summary and Conclusions


Code
display(Markdown(f'''
**Persistence.** Across **{len(counties)}** contiguous-US counties the partisan map barely moved. County GOP two-party share correlates at
**r = {r_persist:.3f}** between 2020 and 2024. Moran's I is **{morans["rep2p_2020"].I:.3f}** and **{morans["rep2p_2024"].I:.3f}**,
and LISA cluster membership carries over (Jaccard HH = **{jaccard(hh20.to_numpy(), hh24.to_numpy()):.2f}**, LL = **{jaccard(ll20.to_numpy(), ll24.to_numpy()):.2f}**).
The same covariates explain both years with nearly identical slopes (R² **{ols["rep2p_2020"].r2:.2f}** vs **{ols["rep2p_2024"].r2:.2f}**).
Rurality and evangelical adherence go with Republican support; college education, Black share, and unemployment go with Democratic support.
That is the durable geography.

**Change.** On top of that stable map, **{(dy > 0).mean() * 100:.0f}%** of counties moved toward the GOP (median **{np.median(dy):+.2f} pp**,
ballot-weighted **{weighted_shift:+.2f} pp**). The move was spatially organised: Moran's I of the shift is **{morans["shift"].I:.3f}**,
and Gi\\* marks **{int(hot.sum())}** hot-spot counties. Those hot spots do not coincide with the persistent GOP core
(Jaccard **{jaccard(hot, (hh20 & hh24).to_numpy()):.2f}**) and overlap more with the persistent Democratic core
(Jaccard **{jaccard(hot, (ll20 & ll24).to_numpy()):.2f}**). The shift's strongest correlate is **{COVAR_LABELS[lead]}**
({shift_slopes[lead]:+.2f} pp per SD), followed by {", ".join(COVAR_LABELS[c] for c in shift_rank[1:4])}.
Education and evangelical adherence, which carry the level models, have shift slopes of only
{shift_slopes["pct_some_college"]:+.2f} and {shift_slopes["pct_evangelical"]:+.2f}.
GWR shows the Hispanic-share association is far from uniform: its local slope on the shift runs from
**{local_focus.min():.2f}** to **{local_focus.max():.2f}** pp per SD, and between 2020 and 2024 the local Hispanic slope on GOP share
rose in **{(counties["gwr_hisp_change"] > 0).mean() * 100:.0f}%** of counties.

**Robustness.** A spatial model (**{spatial_fits["shift"]["best"]}**) beats OLS for every outcome. The count model against a
kept-2020 expectation gives **{(counties["p_right"] > 0.95).sum()}** counties a posterior probability above 0.95 of a real rightward move.
XGBoost scored on held-out states (R² **{r2_cv:.2f}** vs OLS **{r2_cv_ols:.2f}**) ranks {shap_top3} highest and still leaves
spatially autocorrelated residuals (I = **{moran_ml.I:.3f}**).

**Interpretation limits.** These are county-level associations (ecological fallacy). The 2024 returns are provisional and come from a
different compiler than 2020. The covariates describe places, not voters. Two elections are a comparison, not a trend:
`presidential_election_results` already holds 2004–2016 for a longer panel.
'''))


Persistence. Across 3097 contiguous-US counties the partisan map barely moved. County GOP two-party share correlates at r = 0.995 between 2020 and 2024. Moran’s I is 0.607 and 0.602, and LISA cluster membership carries over (Jaccard HH = 0.90, LL = 0.87). The same covariates explain both years with nearly identical slopes (R² 0.62 vs 0.62). Rurality and evangelical adherence go with Republican support; college education, Black share, and unemployment go with Democratic support. That is the durable geography.
Change. On top of that stable map, 88% of counties moved toward the GOP (median +1.53 pp, ballot-weighted +2.39 pp). The move was spatially organised: Moran’s I of the shift is 0.500, and Gi* marks 217 hot-spot counties. Those hot spots do not coincide with the persistent GOP core (Jaccard 0.00) and overlap more with the persistent Democratic core (Jaccard 0.16). The shift’s strongest correlate is % Hispanic (+0.63 pp per SD), followed by Poverty <150% FPL (percentile), % non-Hispanic Black, % unemployed. Education and evangelical adherence, which carry the level models, have shift slopes of only +0.01 and -0.21. GWR shows the Hispanic-share association is far from uniform: its local slope on the shift runs from -3.52 to 3.41 pp per SD, and between 2020 and 2024 the local Hispanic slope on GOP share rose in 71% of counties.
Robustness. A spatial model (SEM) beats OLS for every outcome. The count model against a kept-2020 expectation gives 1906 counties a posterior probability above 0.95 of a real rightward move. XGBoost scored on held-out states (R² 0.36 vs OLS 0.26) ranks % non-Hispanic Black, % Hispanic, Poverty <150% FPL (percentile) highest and still leaves spatially autocorrelated residuals (I = 0.356).
Interpretation limits. These are county-level associations (ecological fallacy). The 2024 returns are provisional and come from a different compiler than 2020. The covariates describe places, not voters. Two elections are a comparison, not a trend: presidential_election_results already holds 2004–2016 for a longer panel.

title: Spatiotemporal Patterns, Hotspots, and Predictors of Crime Across NYC Police Precincts
text:
Overview

Across NYC police precincts from 2000 to 2025, which precincts have the highest crime counts and area rates, are high-crime precincts spatially clustered, how have patterns changed over time, which precincts are persistent or emerging hotspots, and do robbery, burglary, and felony assault share the same geography?


Research objectives







Objective
Research question




1. Crime distribution
Which precincts have the highest crime counts and rates?


2. Spatial clustering
Are high-crime precincts geographically clustered?


3. Temporal trends
How have crime patterns changed over time?


4. Spatiotemporal hotspots
Which precincts experience persistent or emerging crime hotspots?


5. Crime determinants
How are lagged crime, neighboring crime, area exposure, and offense mix associated with crime levels?





Hypotheses

H1: Crime exhibits significant spatial autocorrelation across NYC precincts.
H2: Crime hotspots are persistent in some precincts but shift over time.
H3: Violent and property crimes have different spatial and temporal patterns.
H4: Crime rates exhibit long-term temporal trends (annual panel; monthly seasonality is out of scope here).
H5: Lagged crime, neighboring crime, and other offense activity are associated with crime patterns (socioeconomic ACS covariates are noted as an extension).



Outcomes








Variable
Definition
Role




robbery
Robbery counts
Violent focus outcome


burglery
Burglary counts (Columbia field spelling)
Property focus outcome


assault
Felony assault counts
Violent focus outcome


violent
murder + rape + robbery + assault
Violent composite


property
burglery + gdlarceny + gdlarcauto
Property composite


drug
feldrug + misdrug
Enforcement-activity proxy in the panel models


*_rate
Count per km\(^2\) of precinct area
Exposure-adjusted map / model target


delta_*
2024 minus 2019 count
Recent change





Workflow (guideline section in brackets)







Step
What we do




Data [3, Steps 1-4]
Load GeoPackage panel + SQLite; CRS audit; boundary-vintage audit; harmonized 75-unit panel; composites, boroughs, area rates


Distribution [Step 5]
Choropleths of counts and rates for 2024; fixed-scale maps across years; Leaflet/OSM maps


Temporal [Step 6]
Citywide annual series; borough series; indexed trends by offense; Mann-Kendall tests; precinct-year heatmap; 2019 vs 2024 change


Autocorrelation [Step 7]
Global Moran’s I by year and crime category; Queen, Rook, and KNN sensitivity


Local clusters [Step 8]
LISA (uncorrected and FDR) and Gi* for 2024 levels and the 2019-2024 change; overlap between outcomes


Space-time [Model 6]
Emerging hotspot categories from the Gi* time path for all three outcomes


Cross-section [Models 2-3]
Poisson / negative binomial; OLS, spatial lag, spatial error on 2024 area rates


Panel [Models 1, 2, 4]
Two-way fixed effects; Poisson / negative binomial with fixed effects; dynamic spatial lag panel


Bayesian [Model 5]
BYM relative-risk maps and exceedance probabilities for three five-year windows


Validation [6]
Forward (one-year-ahead) validation and leave-one-borough-out validation


Report
Decision log, caveats, extensions



Caveats. Precinct counts are ecological. Reported crime is not identical to actual crime. Area rates are a proxy for exposure when residential population is unavailable; business and tourist precincts can look extreme under resident-population rates and under area rates for different reasons. Precinct 116 (created Dec 2024) has Excel counts in SQLite but no 2022 geometry in the spatial panel. Precinct 121 (Staten Island) opened in 2013, so full-period analyses use a harmonized geography that merges precincts 120, 121, and 122. The local database is annual, so seasonal analysis and monthly models from the guideline are not attempted.

    "violent": ["murder", "rape", "robbery", "assault"],

print(f"geolattice.spatial_statistics : version {geolattice.spatial_statistics.__version__}")
print(f"gpkg : {GPKG.relative_to(ROOT)}  ({GPKG.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB)")
print(f"sqlite : {DB.relative_to(ROOT)}  ({DB.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB)")

def borough_of(precinct: int) -> str:
    """NYPD precinct numbering: patrol boroughs occupy fixed number ranges."""
    p = int(precinct)
    if p <= 34:
        return "Manhattan"
    if p <= 52:
        return "Bronx"
    if p <= 94:
        return "Brooklyn"
    if p <= 115:
        return "Queens"
    return "Staten Island"

Loaded 77 precincts x 26 years (2000-2025) in EPSG:2263. SQLite long table has 67,694 Excel-sourced offense rows. Mean precinct area is 10.2 km\(^2\).



Harmonize precinct boundaries
The guideline’s Step 2 asks whether precinct boundaries and identifiers changed over the study period. The Columbia catalog layer stores each year with its own polygons, so it can be used to audit the geography behind the 2000-2025 panel, which joins every year to 2022 polygons. Counts for a precinct whose territory changed are not comparable over time unless the geography is harmonized.


Code
# 1) Which precincts exist in each yearly vintage, and did their polygons change?
col = gpd.read_file(GPKG, layer="columbia_precinct_crime_annual")
col["area_km2"] = col.geometry.area * FT2_TO_KM2
n_by_year = col.groupby("year")["precinct"].nunique()
area_w = col.pivot_table(index="precinct", columns="year", values="area_km2")
y0, y1 = int(area_w.columns.min()), int(area_w.columns.max())
vint = pd.DataFrame({f"area_{y0}": area_w[y0], f"area_{y1}": area_w[y1]})
vint["pct_change"] = 100 * (vint[f"area_{y1}"] / vint[f"area_{y0}"] - 1)
changed = vint[(vint["pct_change"].abs() > 1) | vint[f"area_{y0}"].isna()].sort_values("pct_change")
break_years = [int(y) for y in n_by_year.index[n_by_year.diff().fillna(0) != 0]]
print("precincts per year in the Columbia layer:", n_by_year.groupby(n_by_year).agg(lambda s: f"{s.index.min()}-{s.index.max()}").to_dict())
display(Markdown(f"**Precincts whose area differs by more than 1% between the {y0} and {y1} polygons**"))
display(changed.style.format("{:.2f}", na_rep="not yet created"))

# 2) Do the two sources agree where they overlap?
both = col.merge(
    panel[["precinct", "year", *FOCUS_COUNTS]], on=["precinct", "year"], suffixes=("_wfs", "_xls")
)
agree = {c: float((both[f"{c}_wfs"] == both[f"{c}_xls"]).mean()) for c in FOCUS_COUNTS}
print("share of precinct-years where Columbia WFS and NYPD Excel counts are identical:", agree)

# 3) Harmonized geography: merge the Staten Island precincts affected by the 2013 split
count_cols = [
    c for c in panel.select_dtypes("number").columns
    if c not in ("precinct", "year", "area_km2") and not c.endswith("_rate")
]
tab = pd.DataFrame(panel.drop(columns="geometry"))
tab["unit"] = tab["precinct"].replace({p: SI_UNIT for p in SI_MERGE})
tab_h = tab.groupby(["unit", "year"], as_index=False)[count_cols].sum()

geom_h = panel.loc[panel["year"] == panel["year"].max(), ["precinct", "geometry"]].copy()
geom_h["unit"] = geom_h["precinct"].replace({p: SI_UNIT for p in SI_MERGE})
geom_h = geom_h.dissolve(by="unit")[["geometry"]].sort_index()
geom_h["area_km2"] = geom_h.geometry.area * FT2_TO_KM2
geom_h["borough"] = [borough_of(u) for u in geom_h.index]

panel_h = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    tab_h.merge(geom_h.reset_index(), on="unit").rename(columns={"unit": "precinct"}),
    geometry="geometry", crs=panel.crs,
).sort_values(["precinct", "year"]).reset_index(drop=True)
panel_h["drug"] = panel_h["feldrug"] + panel_h["misdrug"]
for c in list(FOCUS_COUNTS) + ["violent", "property", "tot_7major"]:
    panel_h[f"{c}_rate"] = panel_h[c] / panel_h["area_km2"]

units = list(geom_h.index)
years = sorted(int(v) for v in panel_h["year"].unique())
N_U, N_T = len(units), len(years)
assert len(panel_h) == N_U * N_T, "harmonized panel is not balanced"


def mat(column: str, frame: pd.DataFrame = None) -> np.ndarray:
    # Harmonized panel as a (units x years) matrix, rows in `units` order.
    frame = panel_h if frame is None else frame
    return (
        frame.pivot(index="precinct", columns="year", values=column)
        .reindex(index=units, columns=years).to_numpy(float)
    )


raw_rows = panel.groupby("precinct")["year"].nunique()
display(Markdown(

    f"**{int(n_by_year.max())}** from **{break_years[0]}**, when precinct 121 was created from parts of 120 and 122. "
    f"In the 2000-2025 panel **{int((raw_rows < panel['year'].nunique()).sum())}** precinct has an incomplete series, "
    f"and the pre-{break_years[0]} counts of precincts 120 and 122 refer to larger territories than their 2022 polygons. "
    f"Merging {', '.join(str(p) for p in SI_MERGE)} gives a balanced panel of **{N_U}** units x **{N_T}** years "
    f"(**{len(panel_h):,}** rows). Other boundary revisions are smaller (at most "
    f"**{changed.drop(index=[p for p in SI_MERGE if p in changed.index])['pct_change'].abs().max():.0f}%** of a precinct's area) and are left as they are. "
    f"Single-year sections (2019 and 2024) keep all **{panel['precinct'].nunique()}** precincts; "
    f"every full-period section uses the harmonized panel."
))

title: Spatiotemporal Patterns, Hotspots, and Predictors of Crime Across NYC Police Precincts
text:
Interactive Leaflet maps (OpenStreetMap)
Folium builds Leaflet.js maps. Choropleths for 2024 robbery rates and the 2019-2024 robbery change sit on an OpenStreetMap basemap.


Code
def leaflet_choropleth(
    gdf: gpd.GeoDataFrame,
    column: str,
    title: str,
    cmap_name: str = "YlOrRd",
    diverging: bool = False,
    zoom_start: int = 10,
) -> folium.Map:
    """Choropleth on an OpenStreetMap basemap (WGS84)."""
    g = gdf[["precinct", column, "geometry"]].copy()
    g["geometry"] = g.geometry.simplify(30, preserve_topology=True)  # about 9 m; keeps the notebook small
    g = g.to_crs(4326)
    g = g[g.geometry.notna() & ~g.geometry.is_empty].copy()
    g[column] = pd.to_numeric(g[column], errors="coerce")
    g = g.dropna(subset=[column])
    g["precinct"] = g["precinct"].astype(int)
    g["value_label"] = g[column].map(lambda v: f"{v:,.1f}" if abs(v) < 100 else f"{v:,.0f}")

    bounds = g.total_bounds
    center = [float((bounds[1] + bounds[3]) / 2), float((bounds[0] + bounds[2]) / 2)]

    if diverging:
        vmax = float(np.nanmax(np.abs(g[column])))
        vmin, vmax = -vmax, vmax
        colors = ["#2166ac", "#f7f7f7", "#b2182b"]
    else:
        vmin, vmax = float(g[column].min()), float(g[column].max())
        mpl_cmap = plt.get_cmap(cmap_name)
        colors = [
            f"#{int(r * 255):02x}{int(gg * 255):02x}{int(b * 255):02x}"
            for r, gg, b, _a in (mpl_cmap(x) for x in np.linspace(0.15, 0.95, 8))
        ]

    colormap = LinearColormap(colors=colors, vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax, caption=title)
    m = folium.Map(
        location=center, zoom_start=zoom_start, tiles="OpenStreetMap", control_scale=True
    )

    def style_function(feature):
        val = feature["properties"].get(column)
        return {
            "fillColor": colormap(val) if val is not None else "#cccccc",
            "color": "#333333",
            "weight": 0.6,
            "fillOpacity": 0.72,
        }

    folium.GeoJson(
        data=json.loads(g.to_json()),
        name=title,
        style_function=style_function,
        tooltip=folium.GeoJsonTooltip(
            fields=["precinct", "value_label"],
            aliases=["Precinct", title],
            sticky=True,
        ),
        highlight_function=lambda _f: {"weight": 2, "color": "#000000", "fillOpacity": 0.9},
    ).add_to(m)
    colormap.add_to(m)
    folium.LayerControl(collapsed=False).add_to(m)
    return m


m_rate = leaflet_choropleth(
    g_cur, "robbery_rate", f"Robbery rate / km2 ({YEAR_CUR})"
)
m_delta = leaflet_choropleth(
    change, "delta_robbery", f"Change in robbery ({YEAR_BASE}-{YEAR_CUR})", diverging=True
)

title: Spatiotemporal Patterns, Hotspots, and Predictors of Crime Across NYC Police Precincts
text:
Global spatial autocorrelation
Queen contiguity on precinct polygons. Moran’s I is computed each year for robbery, burglary, assault, violent, and property to test H1 and H3. The yearly path uses the harmonized 75-unit panel so that all 26 years are covered; the 2024 scatter and the local statistics use the 77 precincts.


Code
geom = g_cur[["precinct", "geometry"]].copy().reset_index(drop=True)
w = Queen(geom.set_index("precinct"), transform="row")
print(w.summary())
display(Markdown(
    f"Queen weights on **{w.n}** precincts: "
    f"**{len(w.islands())}** island(s), **{w.n_components()}** component(s)."
))

w_h = Queen(geom_h, transform="row")
assert list(w_h.id_order) == units
print(f"harmonized weights: {w_h.n} units, {w_h.n_components()} component(s)")

outcomes = ["robbery", "burglery", "assault", "violent", "property"]
moran_rows = []
for year, sub in panel_h.groupby("year"):
    for col in outcomes:
        s = sub.set_index("precinct")[col].reindex(w_h.id_order)
        if s.isna().any():
            continue
        mi = Moran(s.to_numpy(float), w_h, permutations=PERM, seed=SEED)
        moran_rows.append(
            {"year": int(year), "outcome": col, "I": mi.I, "p_value": mi.p_value, "z_score": mi.z_score}
        )
moran_ts = pd.DataFrame(moran_rows)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.2), constrained_layout=True)
colors = {
    "robbery": "#b22222", "burglery": "#1f4e79", "assault": "#e67e22",
    "violent": "#7f0000", "property": "#08519c",
}
for col, color in colors.items():
    d = moran_ts[moran_ts["outcome"] == col]
    ax.plot(d["year"], d["I"], color=color, lw=1.8, label=col)
ax.axhline(0, color="0.4", lw=0.8)
ax.set_title("Moran's I by crime category, 2000-2025")
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel("Moran's I")
ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=3, fontsize=8)
plt.show()

cur_I = (
    moran_ts[moran_ts["year"] == YEAR_CUR]
    .set_index("outcome")[["I", "p_value", "z_score"]]
    .reindex(outcomes)
)
display(cur_I.style.format({"I": "{:.3f}", "p_value": "{:.3f}", "z_score": "{:.2f}"}))

y_rob = g_cur.set_index("precinct")["robbery"].reindex(w.id_order).to_numpy(float)
mi_rob = Moran(y_rob, w, permutations=PERM, seed=SEED)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 5), constrained_layout=True)
_ = moran_scatter(mi_rob, ax=ax, s=28, alpha=0.75)
ax.set_title(f"Moran scatter - robbery ({YEAR_CUR})")
plt.show()
display(Markdown(
    f"In {YEAR_CUR}, Moran's I for robbery is **{mi_rob.I:.3f}** "
    f"(p = **{mi_rob.p_value:.3f}**). Across {moran_ts['year'].nunique()} years and five outcomes, Moran's I ranges from "
    f"**{moran_ts['I'].min():.2f}** to **{moran_ts['I'].max():.2f}** and is significant at {ALPHA} in **{(moran_ts['p_value'] < ALPHA).mean() * 100:.0f}%** of the outcome-years, supporting H1. "
    f"Mean I over the period is **{moran_ts[moran_ts['outcome'] == 'violent']['I'].mean():.2f}** for the violent composite and "
    f"**{moran_ts[moran_ts['outcome'] == 'property']['I'].mean():.2f}** for the property composite (H3)."
))


Spatial Weights (W)
===================
  Observations        77
  Transform           row
  Min neighbors       1
  Mean neighbors      4.260

text:
Space-time emerging hotspots
Track Gi* hot/cold membership in every year, then classify each unit’s trajectory (new, persistent, intensifying, diminishing, sporadic), following the Part 9.3 emerging-hotspot logic and crime analysis.qmd Section 5 / Model 6. The classification runs on the harmonized panel, so every unit has all 26 years, and is repeated for robbery, burglary, and felony assault. Gi* uses analytic p-values with the FDR adjustment across units.


Code
precincts = units
n_t, n_i = N_T, N_U


def emerging_hotspots(column: str):
    # Gi* membership by year plus a Mann-Kendall trend, classified per unit.
    series = mat(column).T  # (years, units)
    hot_matrix = np.zeros((n_t, n_i), dtype=int)
    cold_matrix = np.zeros((n_t, n_i), dtype=int)
    for t in range(n_t):
        gi = getis_ord_gi(series[t], w_h, star=True, inference="analytic", alpha=ALPHA, seed=SEED)
        labs = np.array([gi_group(x) for x in gi.labels])
        hot_matrix[t] = labs == "Hot spot"
        cold_matrix[t] = labs == "Cold spot"

    mk_rows = []
    for j, pct in enumerate(precincts):
        res = mk.original_test(series[:, j])
        mk_rows.append({
            "precinct": pct, "trend": res.trend, "p": res.p,
            "significant": res.p < ALPHA, "slope": res.slope,
        })
    mk_df = pd.DataFrame(mk_rows).set_index("precinct")

    def categorize(j: int) -> str:
        n_hot, n_cold = hot_matrix[:, j].sum(), cold_matrix[:, j].sum()
        if n_hot > 0 and n_cold > 0:
            return "oscillating"
        if n_hot == 0 and n_cold == 0:
            return "no pattern"
        is_hot = n_hot > 0
        n_x = n_hot if is_hot else n_cold
        m = hot_matrix if is_hot else cold_matrix
        last3, first3 = m[-3:, j].sum(), m[:3, j].sum()
        pct = precincts[j]
        trend_sig = bool(mk_df.loc[pct, "significant"])
        increasing = mk_df.loc[pct, "trend"] == "increasing"
        strengthening = increasing if is_hot else (not increasing)

        if n_x == 1 and last3 >= 1 and first3 == 0:
            label = "new"
        elif n_x >= 0.9 * n_t:
            label = "persistent"
        elif trend_sig and strengthening and last3 >= 2:
            label = "intensifying"
        elif trend_sig and (not strengthening) and first3 >= 1 and last3 == 0:
            label = "diminishing"
        else:
            label = "sporadic"
        return f"{label} {'hot' if is_hot else 'cold'} spot"

    cats = pd.Series([categorize(j) for j in range(n_i)], index=precincts, name="category")
    return cats, hot_matrix, cold_matrix, mk_df

text:
Cross-sectional models for 2024
Cross-section for 2024: explain robbery counts with area exposure (offset), a one-year lag, and property crime as a co-located activity proxy (guideline Model 2). Then fit OLS, spatial lag, and spatial error models on robbery rates (Model 3). The negative binomial dispersion parameter is estimated from the Poisson fit and not fixed at 1. Socioeconomic ACS covariates are the natural next join (guideline Section 2B) and are left as an extension.


Code
# Modeling frame aligned to weight ids
g_lag = year_slice(YEAR_CUR - 1).set_index("precinct").reindex(w.id_order)
mod = g_cur.set_index("precinct").reindex(w.id_order).copy()
mod["robbery_lag"] = g_lag["robbery"].to_numpy()
mod["property"] = g_lag["property"].to_numpy()  # lagged property activity proxy
mod["area_km2"] = mod.geometry.area * FT2_TO_KM2
mod["robbery_rate"] = mod["robbery"] / mod["area_km2"]
mod["log_area"] = np.log(mod["area_km2"])

y = mod["robbery"].to_numpy(float)
X_nb = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "const": 1.0,
        "robbery_lag": mod["robbery_lag"].to_numpy(float),
        "property_lag": mod["property"].to_numpy(float),
    },
    index=mod.index,
)

# Poisson with area offset
poisson = sm.GLM(
    y, X_nb, family=sm.families.Poisson(), offset=mod["log_area"].to_numpy(float)
).fit()
def nb2_alpha(y_obs, mu) -> float:
    # Cameron-Trivedi auxiliary regression: Var(y) = mu + alpha * mu^2.
    z = ((y_obs - mu) ** 2 - y_obs) / mu
    return max(float(np.sum(mu * z) / np.sum(mu ** 2)), 1e-6)


# Negative binomial (NB2) via GLM, with the dispersion estimated from the Poisson fit
alpha_nb = nb2_alpha(y, poisson.mu)
nb_model = sm.GLM(
    y, X_nb, family=sm.families.NegativeBinomial(alpha=alpha_nb),
    offset=mod["log_area"].to_numpy(float),
).fit()

# Spatial lag on rates
X_rate = np.column_stack(
    [
        mod["robbery_lag"].to_numpy(float) / mod["area_km2"].to_numpy(float),
        mod["property"].to_numpy(float) / mod["area_km2"].to_numpy(float),
    ]
)
ols = OLS(
    mod["robbery_rate"].to_numpy(float), X_rate, w=w,
    names=["robbery_lag_rate", "property_lag_rate"], y_name="robbery_rate",
)
sar = SpatialLag(
    mod["robbery_rate"].to_numpy(float), X_rate, w,
    names=["robbery_lag_rate", "property_lag_rate"], y_name="robbery_rate",
)

sem = SpatialError(
    mod["robbery_rate"].to_numpy(float), X_rate, w,
    names=["robbery_lag_rate", "property_lag_rate"], y_name="robbery_rate",
)
lm = ols.lm_tests()

title: Spatiotemporal Patterns, Hotspots, and Predictors of Crime Across NYC Police Precincts
section: Panel models: fixed effects, counts, and a dynamic spatial lag
text:
Panel models: fixed effects, counts, and a dynamic spatial lag
The guideline’s main modeling sequence uses the precinct-time panel. With the harmonized panel (75 units, 2001 to 2025 after one lag) the models are:

Model 1, two-way fixed effects. \(\log(1+Y_{it}) = X_{i,t-1}\beta + \alpha_i + \delta_t + \epsilon_{it}\), with standard errors clustered by unit.
Model 2, Poisson and negative binomial with the same unit and year effects. Precinct area is constant within a unit, so the exposure offset is absorbed by \(\alpha_i\).
Model 4, spatiotemporal lag. \(y_{it} = \rho\sum_j w_{ij}y_{jt} + \phi y_{i,t-1} + X_{i,t-1}\beta + \alpha_i + \delta_t + \epsilon_{it}\), estimated by maximum likelihood on the two-way demeaned data with a block-diagonal weights matrix (one Queen block per year).

No socioeconomic covariates are in the local database, so \(X\) holds two lagged activity measures: the other major felonies in the unit and drug offenses, which largely record enforcement activity. All three focus outcomes are fitted to compare their dynamics (H3).


Code
L = {c: np.log1p(mat(c)) for c in [*FOCUS_COUNTS, "tot_7major", "drug"]}
RAW = {c: mat(c) for c in [*FOCUS_COUNTS, "tot_7major", "drug"]}
T1 = N_T - 1  # usable years after one lag
W_block = W.from_sparse(sparse.kron(sparse.identity(T1), w_h.sparse, format="csr"), transform=None)
unit_id = np.repeat(np.arange(N_U), T1)


def twoway(a):
    # Two-way within transformation of a (units x years) matrix.
    return a - a.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True) - a.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True) + a.mean()


def cluster_ols(yv, Xv):
    # OLS on demeaned data with unit-clustered standard errors.
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(Xv, yv, rcond=None)
    res = yv - Xv @ beta
    bread = np.linalg.inv(Xv.T @ Xv)
    scores = np.zeros((N_U, Xv.shape[1]))
    np.add.at(scores, unit_id, Xv * res[:, None])
    n, k = Xv.shape
    adj = (N_U / (N_U - 1)) * ((n - 1) / (n - N_U - T1 + 1 - k))
    se = np.sqrt(np.diag(bread @ (scores.T @ scores) @ bread) * adj)
    return beta, se, res


panel_rows, count_rows, fits = [], [], {}
for c, label in FOCUS_COUNTS.items():
    other = np.log1p(RAW["tot_7major"] - RAW[c])
    y_m = L[c][:, 1:]
    ylag_m = L[c][:, :-1]
    xo_m = other[:, :-1]
    xd_m = L["drug"][:, :-1]

    yv = twoway(y_m).ravel()
    X_static = np.column_stack([twoway(xo_m).ravel(), twoway(xd_m).ravel()])
    X_dyn = np.column_stack([twoway(ylag_m).ravel(), X_static])

    b1, se1, r1 = cluster_ols(yv, X_static)
    b2, se2, r2 = cluster_ols(yv, X_dyn)
    st = SpatialLag(yv, X_dyn, W_block, add_constant=False,
                    names=["own_lag", "other_felonies_lag", "drug_lag"], y_name=c)
    fits[c] = st
    sst = float(yv @ yv)
    for name, beta, se, res, rho, rho_p in [
        ("M1 two-way FE", np.r_[np.nan, b1], np.r_[np.nan, se1], r1, np.nan, np.nan),
        ("M4a + temporal lag", b2, se2, r2, np.nan, np.nan),
        ("M4b + spatial lag", st.beta, st.se, st.residuals, st.rho, st.spatial_p),
    ]:
        mi_res = Moran(res, W_block, permutations=PERM, seed=SEED)
        panel_rows.append({
            "outcome": label, "model": name,
            "phi (own lag)": beta[0], "se phi": se[0],
            "other felonies (lag)": beta[1], "se other": se[1],
            "drug offenses (lag)": beta[2], "se drug": se[2],
            "rho (spatial lag)": rho, "p rho": rho_p,
            "within R2": 1 - float(res @ res) / sst,
            "resid Moran I": mi_res.I, "p resid": mi_res.p_value,
        })

    # Count models with unit and year effects
    long = pd.DataFrame({
        "y": RAW[c][:, 1:].ravel(),
        "other": xo_m.ravel(), "drug": xd_m.ravel(),
        "unit": np.repeat(units, T1), "year": np.tile(years[1:], N_U),
    })
    D = pd.get_dummies(long[["unit", "year"]].astype(str), drop_first=True, dtype=float)
    Xc = sm.add_constant(pd.concat([long[["other", "drug"]], D], axis=1))
    pois = sm.GLM(long["y"], Xc, family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit()
    a_hat = nb2_alpha(long["y"].to_numpy(float), pois.mu)
    nbfe = sm.GLM(long["y"], Xc, family=sm.families.NegativeBinomial(alpha=a_hat)).fit()
    count_rows.append({
        "outcome": label,
        "Poisson dispersion": pois.pearson_chi2 / pois.df_resid,
        "NB alpha": a_hat,
        "Poisson AIC": pois.aic, "NB AIC": nbfe.aic,
        "NB other felonies (lag)": nbfe.params["other"], "p other": nbfe.pvalues["other"],
        "NB drug offenses (lag)": nbfe.params["drug"], "p drug": nbfe.pvalues["drug"],
    })

panel_tbl = pd.DataFrame(panel_rows).set_index(["outcome", "model"])
display(Markdown("### Linear panel models on log(1 + count)"))
display(panel_tbl.style.format("{:.3f}", na_rep=""))
count_tbl = pd.DataFrame(count_rows).set_index("outcome")
display(Markdown("### Count models with unit and year fixed effects"))
display(count_tbl.style.format({
    "Poisson dispersion": "{:.2f}", "NB alpha": "{:.4f}", "Poisson AIC": "{:,.0f}", "NB AIC": "{:,.0f}",
    "NB other felonies (lag)": "{:.3f}", "p other": "{:.4f}", "NB drug offenses (lag)": "{:.3f}", "p drug": "{:.4f}",
}))

s4 = panel_tbl.xs("M4b + spatial lag", level="model")
s1 = panel_tbl.xs("M1 two-way FE", level="model")
display(Markdown(
    f"Temporal persistence (phi) is **{s4.loc['Robbery', 'phi (own lag)']:.2f}** for robbery, "
    f"**{s4.loc['Burglary', 'phi (own lag)']:.2f}** for burglary, and **{s4.loc['Felony assault', 'phi (own lag)']:.2f}** for felony assault. "
    f"The contemporaneous spatial lag (rho) is **{s4.loc['Robbery', 'rho (spatial lag)']:.2f}**, "
    f"**{s4.loc['Burglary', 'rho (spatial lag)']:.2f}**, and **{s4.loc['Felony assault', 'rho (spatial lag)']:.2f}** "
    f"(p = {s4.loc['Robbery', 'p rho']:.3g}, {s4.loc['Burglary', 'p rho']:.3g}, {s4.loc['Felony assault', 'p rho']:.3g}): "
    f"after removing unit and year effects, a unit's crime still moves with its neighbors' in the same year. "
    f"Residual Moran's I for robbery is **{s1.loc['Robbery', 'resid Moran I']:.3f}** in the static model and "
    f"**{s4.loc['Robbery', 'resid Moran I']:.3f}** with both lags: the positive clustering is gone and a small negative value remains. "
    f"Poisson dispersion is **{count_tbl['Poisson dispersion'].min():.1f}** to **{count_tbl['Poisson dispersion'].max():.1f}**, "
    f"so the negative binomial is preferred for the counts. "
    f"A fixed-effects model with a lagged outcome is biased downward in phi for short panels (about 1/T, here T = {T1}), "
    f"and rho measures co-movement, not a causal spillover."
))
